articles.title: How to set up the corporate VPN on a company laptop
articles.body:
The corporate VPN gives you secure access to internal systems — the ticketing portal, shared file stores, and staging environments — when you work from home, a client site, or any network outside the office. Because our regional offices connect over public internet links, the VPN is mandatory whenever you touch internal resources from an untrusted network. This article explains how to install, connect, and troubleshoot the client on a company-managed laptop.

Before you begin, confirm two things. First, your laptop must already be enrolled in device management (see the provisioning guide) so that the VPN configuration profile is pushed automatically. Second, you must have completed MFA enrollment, because the VPN requires a second factor at every login. If either step is missing, the connection will fail with an authorization error rather than a network error.

Installing the client is usually automatic. On managed devices the VPN agent appears in your applications folder within an hour of first enrollment. If it is not present, open the self-service software catalog and search for "Corporate VPN Client," then click Install. Do not download a VPN client from a public website — only the catalog build is configured with the correct gateway and certificate settings.

To connect for the first time:

- Launch the VPN client and select the profile named after your region (for example, "APAC-Primary").
- Enter your standard directory username. Do not include a domain prefix.
- Enter your directory password, then approve the push notification on your enrolled MFA device.
- Wait for the status indicator to turn green and read "Connected."

Once connected, all traffic to internal hostnames under *.internal.example is routed through the encrypted tunnel, while ordinary internet browsing continues to use your local connection. This split-tunnel design keeps video calls and public sites fast while still protecting internal access. You do not need to disconnect the VPN to join a normal web meeting.

A few operational notes will save you time. The VPN session has a maximum lifetime of twelve hours, after which you will be prompted to re-authenticate. This is expected behavior, not a fault. If your laptop goes to sleep, the client reconnects automatically on wake, but you may need to re-approve the MFA prompt. When you switch networks — for instance, moving from home Wi-Fi to a mobile hotspot — allow a few seconds for the tunnel to rebuild before retrying a failed request.

Troubleshooting the most common problems:

- "Authentication failed" but the password is correct: your MFA approval likely timed out. Reconnect and approve the prompt within thirty seconds.
- "Cannot reach gateway": your underlying internet connection is down or a captive portal (hotel or airport Wi-Fi) is intercepting traffic. Open a browser, complete the portal sign-in, then retry.
- Internal sites load slowly or not at all while connected: flush your DNS cache and reconnect. If it persists, note the hostname and open a ticket.
- The client shows "Profile not found": your device enrollment did not complete. Contact the service desk to re-push the configuration.

Security expectations are simple but non-negotiable. Never share your VPN credentials, never attempt to route a personal or unmanaged device through the corporate profile, and never disable the client's certificate validation even if prompted by a warning page — a certificate warning on the VPN gateway is a signal to stop and report, not to click through. If you lose your laptop or suspect your credentials are compromised, report it immediately so the session can be revoked.

If the VPN still will not connect after these steps, raise a ticket in the service portal with the exact error text, your region profile name, and the network you are on. The networking team can see gateway-side logs and will usually resolve access issues within one business day. For a total outage affecting many users, follow the incident escalation process rather than filing individual tickets.

articles.title: Enrolling in multi-factor authentication (MFA) for your account
articles.body:
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) protects your account by requiring a second proof of identity in addition to your password. Even if a password is guessed or stolen, an attacker cannot sign in without your second factor. MFA is required for every employee and contractor before accessing email, the VPN, the ticketing portal, or any internal application. This guide walks you through enrolling your first factor and setting up a backup.

We support two primary methods: an authenticator app that generates time-based codes or push approvals, and a hardware security key. We strongly recommend the authenticator app as your primary method because it works offline and does not depend on mobile signal or SMS delivery. SMS one-time codes are not offered as a primary factor because they are the weakest option; do not request them.

To enroll with an authenticator app:

- Install a reputable authenticator app on your phone from your device's official app store.
- On a computer, sign in to the identity portal at id.internal.example and open Security settings.
- Choose "Add authenticator app." A QR code will appear on screen.
- In the app, choose "Add account" and scan the QR code.
- Enter the six-digit code the app shows to confirm the pairing.

Once paired, the portal will ask you to choose between push approvals and manual codes. Push approvals are more convenient: at each sign-in you simply tap Approve. If you travel to areas with poor connectivity, manual codes are a reliable fallback because they are generated on the device itself. You can use both.

After your primary factor is set, immediately register a backup. Accounts with only one factor are the most common reason people get locked out. Your backup can be a second device running the authenticator app, a hardware security key kept in a safe place, or a set of one-time recovery codes. If you generate recovery codes, print them or store them in an approved password manager — never in a plain text file, a note app, or an email to yourself.

Hardware security keys are recommended for anyone with elevated access, such as administrators and finance approvers. To register one, insert or tap the key when the portal prompts "Add security key," then follow the on-screen instruction to touch the key. Register a second key as backup and store it separately.

A few things to know about daily use. You will not be prompted for MFA on every single action; trusted sessions on managed devices may last several hours before asking again. However, high-risk actions — changing your password, adding a new device, or approving a payment — will always re-prompt. This is deliberate. If you ever receive an MFA push you did not initiate, deny it and report it right away, because it means someone has your password.

Common issues and fixes:

- Codes are rejected as invalid: your phone clock has drifted. Enable automatic date and time on the device, which keeps the code generator in sync.
- You replaced your phone and lost the app: use a backup factor to sign in, then remove the old device and enroll the new one. If you have no backup, contact the service desk for identity-verified recovery.
- Push notifications never arrive: confirm the app has notification permission and background data enabled, or switch to manual codes.

If you are completely locked out with no working factor, do not create a new account. Contact the service desk, which will verify your identity through an approved process before resetting your factors. Never ask a colleague to approve a prompt on your behalf, and never read a code aloud to anyone who calls you claiming to be support — legitimate staff will never ask for it.

articles.title: New laptop provisioning and first-day setup for employees
articles.body:
This guide explains what happens when you receive a company laptop and how to complete first-day setup so you can work securely from the start. Every laptop we issue is enrolled in central device management before it reaches you, which means security policies, the VPN profile, and the software catalog are applied automatically. Your job on day one is to sign in, confirm enrollment, and install the tools your role needs.

Provisioning begins before your start date. When your manager submits a hire request, the endpoint team images a device, assigns it to your identity, and ships or hands it over. Each device has an asset tag — a short identifier on a sticker — which links the hardware to you in our inventory. Keep this tag readable; you will need it whenever you contact support or return the device. Do not remove or cover it.

When you first power on the laptop, connect to a network and sign in with your directory username and temporary password. You will be required to change the temporary password immediately and to complete MFA enrollment before you reach the desktop. This ordering is intentional: the device cannot pull down internal software until your identity is verified. If you have not yet received credentials, your manager or the service desk can release them once your start date is active.

After sign-in, confirm the device is managed. Open the self-service software catalog; if it launches and lists applications, enrollment succeeded. If the catalog is missing, restart once and wait ten minutes, since some policies apply on a delayed cycle. If it is still absent, open a ticket with your asset tag so the team can re-enroll the device remotely.

Install the essentials from the catalog rather than from public websites, so that you always get the correctly configured, licensed build. A typical first-day set includes:

- The corporate VPN client, for access to internal systems off the office network.
- The communication and calendar suite used across the company.
- The password manager, which stores your credentials and recovery codes safely.
- Any role-specific tools listed on your team's onboarding page.

Security settings are enforced automatically and should not be disabled. Full-disk encryption is on by default, the screen locks after a short idle period, and updates install on a managed schedule. If an update requires a restart, save your work and allow it promptly rather than deferring repeatedly; deferred updates are the most common cause of avoidable security gaps and, eventually, forced restarts at inconvenient times.

A few practical habits will keep your device healthy. Restart at least once a week so that queued updates finish applying. Keep at least a few gigabytes of free disk space, because backups and updates need room to work. Store work files in the approved cloud location rather than only on the local disk, so that nothing is lost if the hardware fails. And never install software that bypasses the catalog for business use — if a tool you need is missing, raise a software request rather than downloading an unmanaged copy.

If your laptop is lost or stolen, report it immediately through the service desk or the incident process. A managed device can be locked and wiped remotely, which protects company data, but only if we know quickly. Similarly, if the device is damaged, do not attempt repairs yourself; open a hardware ticket with the asset tag and a short description, and the team will arrange a replacement or repair.

When you leave a role or the company, return the laptop through the offboarding process. Do not wipe or reset it yourself — the endpoint team retires the asset, confirms data handling, and updates inventory. Following this process keeps our records accurate and ensures the next person can be provisioned quickly.

articles.title: Reset your own password using the self-service portal
articles.body:
If you have forgotten your password or your account is locked, you can usually fix it yourself in a few minutes using the self-service password reset portal, without waiting for the service desk. This article explains how self-service reset works, how to prepare so it is available when you need it, and what to do if you cannot use it.

Self-service reset works because your account is linked to verified recovery factors — the same authenticator app or security key you registered during MFA enrollment. When you request a reset, the system confirms your identity through those factors before letting you choose a new password. This is why enrolling a backup factor matters: without at least one working factor, self-service cannot verify you, and you will have to fall back to an identity-verified reset by the service desk.

To reset a forgotten password:

- Go to the identity portal at id.internal.example and choose "Can't sign in?"
- Enter your directory username.
- Approve the verification prompt on your authenticator app, or tap your registered security key.
- Choose a new password that meets the policy shown on screen.
- Confirm, then sign in with the new password on your other applications.

If your account is locked rather than forgotten, the cause is usually several failed sign-in attempts — often from an old password saved on your phone's mail app or on the VPN client. Unlocking follows the same flow: verify with a factor, then set a fresh password, and remember to update every device that stored the old one. A single stale saved password will re-lock your account within minutes, so clearing it everywhere is the real fix.

Password policy is designed to be strong but memorable. Aim for a long passphrase rather than a short, complex string; length defeats guessing far more effectively than swapping letters for symbols. Do not reuse a password from any personal account, and never reuse a previous work password. The system keeps a history and will reject recent ones. The best practice is to let the approved password manager generate and store the new password so you never have to type or remember it manually.

There are situations where self-service will not work, and knowing them in advance saves frustration:

- You have no enrolled factor, or lost access to all of them. In this case the service desk must verify your identity through an approved process before resetting.
- Your account has been administratively disabled — for example during an active security review. Self-service is intentionally blocked here; contact the service desk.
- You are trying to reset from a captive network (hotel or airport Wi-Fi) that has not been signed into. Complete the portal sign-in first, then retry.

A word on security. No one from the service desk will ever call and ask you to read out a code, approve a prompt, or tell them your password so they can "reset it for you." Real resets are always performed by you at the portal or through a verified identity check that you initiate. If you receive such a call or message, deny any prompts and report it, because it is almost certainly an attempt to hijack your account.

Finally, prepare now so a future lockout is a minor event. Confirm you have at least two working MFA factors, store recovery codes in the password manager, and make sure your recovery contact details in the portal are current. Employees who do this resolve their own lockouts in minutes; those who do not often wait for a manual identity check. If self-service genuinely cannot help you, open a ticket or call the service desk, and have your asset tag or username ready to speed up verification.

articles.title: Troubleshooting office printer and print queue problems
articles.body:
Print problems are among the most common workplace tickets, and most of them can be solved at your desk in a couple of minutes. This guide walks through the usual causes — from a job stuck in the queue to a printer that has dropped off the network — and tells you when to escalate to Workplace Services.

Our office printers are shared, network-connected multifunction devices reached through managed print queues. When you print, your job goes to a queue and is released either automatically or, on secure printers, when you tap your badge at the device. Understanding this flow helps you diagnose problems: if a job never appears at the printer, the issue is usually between your laptop and the queue; if the job appears but will not print, the issue is usually at the device itself.

Start with the fast checks, which resolve the majority of cases:

- Confirm you selected the correct printer. Devices are named by floor and area (for example, "L3-East-MFP"), and it is easy to send a job to a printer on another floor.
- Check the printer's own screen for a message. "Out of paper," "Low toner," or "Tray open" are self-explanatory and often fixable on the spot.
- If nothing prints, cancel your stuck job and resend a single page. A malformed or oversized document can jam the whole queue behind it.
- Restart the print spooler on your laptop, or simply reboot, which clears most client-side glitches.

If your job is stuck in the queue and will not clear, open your device's printer settings, select the queue, and cancel all documents. A single failed job can block everything behind it, so clearing the queue and resending one document at a time both fixes the jam and identifies the problematic file. Very large files, unusual fonts, or complex graphics are frequent culprits; exporting to PDF before printing often resolves them.

For secure badge-release printers, remember that jobs expire if you do not release them within a set window — commonly a few hours. If you sent a document earlier and it is no longer at the device, it has likely expired and simply needs resending. If your badge is not recognized at the reader, the problem is your badge or the reader rather than the print system, and you should raise a facilities or access ticket instead.

When the printer is offline for everyone nearby, not just you, the device has probably lost its network connection or needs attention only on-site staff can give. Before escalating, confirm it is a shared problem by asking a colleague to try, and note the exact device name from its label. A jam, an empty toner cartridge, or a paper tray that needs refilling can often be cleared by following the illustrated steps on the printer's own screen, and consumables like paper and toner are stocked near most print areas.

Some problems are not yours to fix and should go straight to a ticket:

- Repeated paper jams after clearing, which suggest a worn roller needing service.
- Streaks, faded output, or color banding that persist after a toner change, which indicate a hardware fault.
- A printer that stays offline after a power cycle by facilities staff.
- Any need for a new device, a driver for an unusual format, or access to a restricted printer.

When you open a ticket, include the device name from its label, the floor and area, what you already tried, and whether colleagues are affected too. This lets Workplace Services decide immediately whether to dispatch on-site help or fix a queue centrally, and it avoids a slow back-and-forth. For a printer that is only slow or occasionally misbehaving, a single ticket is enough; there is no need to file one per failed job.

Finally, a note on data care: if you print sensitive material, use secure badge release so pages are not left sitting in the tray, and collect confidential output immediately. Uncollected printouts are a common and avoidable source of information leaks.

articles.title: How to Report a Phishing or Suspicious Email
articles.body:
Phishing remains the most common way attackers gain a foothold at Acme. A single click on a malicious link or a reused password entered into a fake login page can expose customer data and internal systems. Reporting a suspicious message quickly is one of the highest-impact things any employee can do, and there is never a penalty for reporting something that turns out to be legitimate.

You should treat a message as suspicious whenever it asks you to act urgently, requests credentials or payment, contains an unexpected attachment, or comes from a sender whose address does not match the display name. Messages that impersonate leadership ("I need this done now, don't call me") or that spoof internal tools with lookalike domains are especially common. When in doubt, do not click, do not reply, and do not open attachments.

To report, use the built-in reporting button first. In the mail client, select the message and click Report Phishing on the toolbar. This forwards the full message, including headers, to the Security Operations team and removes it from your inbox. If the button is unavailable, forward the message as an attachment to phish-report@acme-internal.example so that the original headers are preserved; a plain forward strips information the analysts need. You can also raise a ticket at support.acme-internal.example if you already interacted with the message and need urgent help.

If you believe you already clicked a link or entered your credentials, act immediately rather than waiting for a response:

- Disconnect the device from the network (turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the cable).
- Change your password from a different, trusted device.
- Report the incident through support.acme-internal.example and mark it urgent.
- Do not delete the suspicious email; Security Operations needs it for investigation.

After you report, the Security Operations team triages the message, checks whether other employees received it, blocks malicious senders and domains, and removes copies from all mailboxes. You may receive a short follow-up asking what you clicked or entered. Answer honestly and completely, even if you feel embarrassed. Attackers rely on people staying silent; fast, candid reporting is what limits the damage.

A few practical habits reduce your exposure. Hover over links before clicking to preview the real destination, and be suspicious of any domain that is a slight misspelling of a known one. Verify unusual payment or data requests through a second channel, such as a direct message or a phone call to a known contact, never using the contact details supplied in the suspicious message itself. Be extra cautious with messages that arrive outside normal working hours or that pressure you to bypass a normal approval step.

Text messages and chat platforms are also common phishing channels. The same rules apply: do not tap unknown links, and report smishing (SMS phishing) and suspicious chat messages the same way, forwarding a screenshot to phish-report@acme-internal.example when a reporting button is not available.

Security Operations publishes a monthly summary of reported campaigns so teams can recognize current tactics. Reporting is not just self-protection; every report improves the filters that protect your colleagues. If you are ever unsure whether something qualifies, report it anyway. Over-reporting costs a few seconds of an analyst's time; under-reporting can cost the company a breach.

articles.title: Data Classification Levels and How to Label Documents
articles.body:
Every piece of information Acme creates or handles carries a level of sensitivity, and how we store, share, and dispose of it must match that level. Data classification gives everyone a shared vocabulary so that the right controls are applied consistently. Acme uses four levels: Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted.

Public information is approved for release outside the company. Examples include published marketing material, press releases, and open documentation. No harm results from disclosure, but only authorized owners may move data into the Public tier, because reclassifying downward is a deliberate decision.

Internal information is the default for day-to-day work. It is not secret, but it is not meant for outsiders: project plans, internal wiki pages, team meeting notes, and org charts. Internal data may be shared freely among employees and approved contractors but should not be posted publicly or sent to third parties without a business reason.

Confidential information could cause real harm if disclosed. This includes customer records, contracts, unpublished financials, source code, and security configurations. Confidential data must be shared on a need-to-know basis, stored only in approved systems, and never placed in personal cloud accounts or unmanaged devices.

Restricted information is the most sensitive tier and would cause serious damage if exposed. Examples include authentication secrets, encryption keys, regulated personal data, and material non-public business information. Restricted data requires access approval, encryption at rest and in transit, and detailed access logging. Access is granted narrowly and reviewed regularly.

Use these guidelines when deciding how to handle each level:

- Public: shareable externally; no special storage controls.
- Internal: employees and approved contractors only; approved systems.
- Confidential: need-to-know; approved systems; no personal devices or accounts.
- Restricted: explicit approval, encryption, logging, and periodic access review.

Labeling makes classification visible. For documents, place the level in the header or footer, for example "Confidential — Acme Internal." In spreadsheets and slide decks, add the label to the title slide or first tab. For structured data and repositories, record the classification in the system's metadata or the repository README. When a document mixes levels, classify it at the highest level present; a mostly-Internal report that contains one Confidential table is Confidential as a whole.

Sharing rules follow the label. Before sending anything outside your immediate team, check the classification and the recipient. External sharing of Confidential or Restricted data requires a business justification and, where applicable, a signed agreement with the receiving party. Never move Confidential or Restricted data into personal email, personal cloud storage, or messaging apps that are not on the approved list at handbook.acme-internal.example.

Retention and disposal also depend on level. Confidential and Restricted data should be deleted or securely archived once it is no longer needed, following the retention schedule. Do not keep sensitive exports on your laptop longer than necessary, and empty local download folders regularly.

When you are unsure how to classify something, choose the more protective level and ask the data owner or the Security team through support.acme-internal.example. It is always safer to over-protect than to under-protect. Classification is not bureaucracy for its own sake; it is the mechanism that lets us collaborate quickly on ordinary work while keeping the small amount of genuinely sensitive information tightly controlled.

articles.title: Device Encryption Requirements for Laptops and Phones
articles.body:
Any device that stores or accesses Acme information must have full-disk encryption enabled. Encryption ensures that if a laptop or phone is lost or stolen, the data on it cannot be read without the correct credentials. This is a baseline requirement for all company-managed devices and for personal devices that are approved to access company systems.

Encryption protects data at rest: the files sitting on the drive when the device is powered off or locked. It does not protect an unlocked, logged-in device, which is why encryption always works together with a strong screen lock and automatic timeout. A stolen encrypted laptop that is left logged in offers little protection, so the two controls are mandatory together.

On company-managed laptops, encryption is enabled and enforced automatically by the device management platform. On Windows machines this uses the built-in disk encryption with keys escrowed to the management system; on macOS it uses the built-in volume encryption. You do not need to configure anything, but you must not disable it. If you see a prompt suggesting encryption is turned off, or your device asks you to defer encryption, contact support.acme-internal.example rather than dismissing it.

Mobile phones and tablets that access company mail or applications must also be encrypted and protected by a passcode or biometric lock. Modern smartphones encrypt storage by default once a passcode is set, so the key requirement is that you set a strong passcode of at least six digits, or better, an alphanumeric one, and enable biometric unlock. Devices without a passcode are not permitted to enroll in company services.

Follow these requirements for every device that touches Acme data:

- Full-disk or full-volume encryption must be enabled and must stay enabled.
- A screen lock with automatic timeout of no more than five minutes.
- A passcode of at least six characters and, where available, biometric unlock.
- Recovery keys stored only in the approved escrow system, never in a text file on the device.
- Removable drives and USB sticks holding company data must be encrypted or avoided entirely.

Recovery keys deserve special attention. If encryption locks you out after a hardware change or forgotten password, the recovery key restores access. For managed devices, this key is automatically escrowed to the management platform, and the support team can retrieve it for you after identity verification. Never store a recovery key in a plain document, a sticky note, or a personal notes app, because that defeats the purpose of encryption.

External media is a frequent gap. USB flash drives, portable SSDs, and SD cards are easy to lose and rarely encrypted. Avoid putting Confidential or Restricted data on removable media at all; use approved cloud storage instead. When removable media is genuinely necessary, use hardware-encrypted drives issued by IT.

If a device is lost or stolen, report it immediately through support.acme-internal.example so it can be remotely locked or wiped and its access revoked. Encryption buys time, but a prompt remote wipe closes the risk entirely. Do not wait until the end of the day or assume you will find it; report first, search second.

Encryption is invisible when it works and invaluable when it matters. Keeping it enabled costs you nothing in daily use and protects both you and every customer whose data might otherwise sit unprotected on a misplaced device.

articles.title: Handling Secrets, API Keys, and Passwords Safely
articles.body:
Secrets are the keys to Acme's systems: passwords, API keys, database credentials, access tokens, private certificates, and encryption keys. A leaked secret can give an attacker the same access as a trusted employee or service, so handling secrets carefully is one of the most important security disciplines for every team, not just engineers.

The first rule is that secrets never belong in source code, configuration files committed to a repository, chat messages, tickets, or documents. A secret pasted into a code review or a wiki page is effectively public, because it persists in history and backups long after the message is deleted. Instead, secrets live in the approved secrets manager, where they are encrypted, access-controlled, and audited. Applications read them at runtime from the secrets manager or from injected environment variables, never from hard-coded values.

For personal credentials, use the company-provided password manager to generate and store unique passwords. Every account should have a distinct, long, randomly generated password; reusing a password across systems means one breach compromises many. Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) everywhere it is offered, and prefer an authenticator app or hardware key over SMS codes, which can be intercepted.

Apply these practices to every secret you touch:

- Store secrets only in the approved secrets manager or password manager, never in code, tickets, or chat.
- Use unique, generated values; never reuse a password or key across systems.
- Grant each service its own credential so access can be revoked individually.
- Rotate secrets on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure.
- Enable MFA on every account that supports it.

Rotation matters because secrets accumulate risk over time. Set keys to expire and rotate them regularly, and rotate immediately if a laptop is lost, an employee with access leaves, or a secret may have been exposed. Automated rotation through the secrets manager is preferred, since manual rotation is easy to forget.

Scope every secret as narrowly as possible. An API key that can only read a single resource is far safer than one with full administrative rights. When creating credentials for a service or integration, request the minimum permissions needed and a separate key per integration so that revoking one does not break everything else. Avoid shared accounts; when a system truly requires one, its credential must live in the secrets manager with access logged.

If you discover a secret in the wrong place, for example an API key committed to a repository or pasted into a chat, treat it as compromised even if you think no one saw it. Report it through support.acme-internal.example, rotate the secret immediately, and let the Security team check for any misuse. Do not simply delete the message or commit; removing it from view does not remove it from history, and the only safe fix is rotation.

Be cautious with secrets in logs and error messages, a common accidental leak. Never log credentials, tokens, or full request headers that contain authorization data. When sharing logs for debugging, redact any secret values first.

Secrets are powerful precisely because systems trust them completely. That trust is only safe when secrets stay in controlled storage, are unique and narrowly scoped, and are rotated the moment their safety is in doubt. Building these habits protects not only your own accounts but the customer data and infrastructure that depend on them.

articles.title: Secure Remote Work: Wi-Fi, VPN, and Home Setup
articles.body:
Working outside the office, whether from home, a co-working space, or while travelling, expands the number of places Acme data can be exposed. The controls that protect you in the office do not all follow you automatically, so remote work carries a few extra responsibilities. Following them keeps company and customer data safe wherever you happen to be.

Start with your network. Home Wi-Fi should use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption with a strong, unique router password, and the default administrator password on the router itself should be changed. Public Wi-Fi in cafes, airports, and hotels should be treated as untrusted; anyone on the same network may attempt to intercept traffic. When you must use public Wi-Fi, connect through the company VPN before doing any work, or use your phone's personal hotspot instead, which is generally safer than open networks.

The VPN is your secure tunnel back to Acme systems. Connect to it whenever you access internal applications, and leave it connected for the duration of your work session. The VPN encrypts your traffic and applies company security policies. If the VPN fails to connect or behaves oddly, stop accessing internal systems and raise a ticket at support.acme-internal.example rather than working around it.

Physical security matters as much as network security when you work in public. Screens are readable by the people around you, and an unattended laptop can be stolen in seconds.

- Never leave a device unattended in a public place, even briefly.
- Lock your screen every time you step away, using a keyboard shortcut out of habit.
- Use a privacy screen filter when working on sensitive material in public.
- Position yourself so that no one can shoulder-surf your screen or keyboard.
- Avoid sensitive video calls in spaces where others can overhear customer or company details.

Keep work on work devices. Do not use a personal computer for company tasks unless it is explicitly approved and enrolled in device management, because personal machines may lack encryption, current patches, and endpoint protection. Likewise, do not move company files into personal email or personal cloud storage to "work on them later"; use the approved collaboration tools, which remain protected and recoverable.

Keep everything updated. Apply operating system and application updates promptly, since remote devices are more exposed and updates often patch actively exploited flaws. Restart when prompted so that pending updates finish installing. Ensure endpoint protection is running and not disabled.

Household sharing is a subtle risk. Do not let family members or housemates use your work laptop, and keep it locked when you are not at it. Voice assistants and smart-home devices can capture audio, so be mindful during confidential calls. When printing at home is unavoidable, retrieve documents immediately and shred anything sensitive rather than leaving it in a recycling bin.

When travelling, be especially careful crossing borders and staying in hotels. Keep devices with you rather than in checked luggage, avoid hotel business-center computers entirely, and be cautious about charging from unknown USB ports, which can carry data risks; use a power adapter into a wall socket instead.

If anything goes wrong, a lost device, a suspicious connection, or a sense that something is off, report it promptly through support.acme-internal.example. Remote work depends on trust, and that trust holds as long as everyone applies the same care to their kitchen table that they would to their office desk.

articles.title: Security Incident Response Runbook: What to Do in the First Hour
articles.body:
A security incident is any event that may compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of Acme systems or data: a confirmed malware infection, a leaked credential, unauthorized access, a lost device holding sensitive data, or a data exposure. This runbook describes what happens in the critical first hour, when fast, calm action limits the damage. The guiding principle is to contain first and investigate second, while preserving evidence.

Anyone can declare an incident, and doing so early is encouraged. If you suspect something is wrong, raise it through support.acme-internal.example marked urgent, or use the security escalation channel. Do not wait until you are certain; a false alarm costs little, while a delayed report can let an attacker spread. When you report, describe what you observed, when, and which systems or accounts are involved.

Once an incident is declared, the on-call Security Operations engineer becomes the incident lead and coordinates the response. The lead assigns roles: someone to drive containment, someone to keep a timeline, and a communications point of contact. Everyone else supports the lead and avoids taking independent action that could destroy evidence or tip off an attacker.

The first-hour priorities follow a clear order:

- Contain: isolate affected devices from the network, disable compromised accounts, and revoke exposed credentials and tokens.
- Preserve: do not power off or wipe affected systems unless instructed; capture logs, screenshots, and the time of each action.
- Assess: determine what was accessed, which data classification levels are involved, and whether the incident is ongoing.
- Communicate: keep stakeholders informed through the designated point of contact only, using approved channels.
- Record: maintain a running timeline of events and decisions for the post-incident review.

Containment is deliberately blunt in the early stage. Disconnecting a laptop from the network, suspending an account, or rotating a key stops the bleeding even before the full picture is clear. The incident lead decides these actions; individual responders should propose steps rather than acting unilaterally, so that evidence is not lost and efforts are not duplicated.

Evidence preservation is easy to overlook under pressure. Avoid rebooting or reimaging a compromised machine, because volatile data such as running processes and memory may be needed to understand what happened. Take screenshots, export relevant logs, and note timestamps in a shared timeline document. If you took an action, record exactly what you did and when.

Communication during an incident must be controlled. Only the designated communications contact speaks to parties outside the response team, and never through the potentially compromised systems. Do not speculate about cause or blame in wide channels, and do not notify customers or external parties on your own; that decision belongs to leadership and, where regulations apply, follows a defined legal and notification process.

When the immediate threat is contained, the response moves from urgency to recovery: restoring systems from known-good backups, resetting affected credentials broadly, applying patches, and verifying that the attacker no longer has access before returning systems to normal use. Recovery is confirmed by the incident lead, not assumed.

Every incident closes with a blameless post-incident review within a week. The review reconstructs the timeline, identifies the root cause, and produces concrete follow-up actions to prevent recurrence. The goal is learning, not blame; people who report and respond honestly make the whole company safer. Keeping this runbook familiar, before you need it, is what turns a stressful hour into a controlled response.

articles.title: New Hire First-Day Checklist: What to Complete in Your First 24 Hours
articles.body:
Welcome to Acme. This checklist covers everything you need to complete during your first day so that you are set up to work productively by the end of the week. Your onboarding buddy and your manager are the two people you should lean on if anything below is unclear; you do not need to solve setup problems alone.

Before you start any task, confirm you have received your welcome email from the People Operations team. It contains your employee ID, your temporary account credentials, and the link to the self-service portal at portal.acme-internal.example. If the email has not arrived by 9:30 on your start date, raise a ticket through the onboarding help desk rather than waiting.

Your first block of the morning is account and identity setup. Complete these steps in order, because several depend on the account created in step one:

- Activate your Acme account and set a permanent password that meets the security policy (minimum length, no reuse of prior passwords).
- Enroll at least two multi-factor authentication methods, for example an authenticator app plus a backup method.
- Sign in to email, the chat workspace, and the document store to confirm access is provisioned.
- Upload a profile photo and confirm your display name and preferred pronouns in the directory.
- Review and acknowledge the acceptable-use and information-security policies in the portal.

Once your accounts are live, move to hardware and workspace. If you are office-based, collect your laptop and access badge from the workplace desk on your floor; if you are remote, confirm that your equipment was delivered and that the asset tag matches the one listed in your welcome email. Run the guided device-setup wizard, which installs required security tooling and the standard application set. Do not install unmanaged software on your work device; request anything you need through the software catalog.

The middle of your day is reserved for orientation. You will have a scheduled session with People Operations covering payroll, benefits enrollment windows, leave policy, and how to reach support. Have your banking details and any tax or residency documents ready so payroll can be set up without a follow-up. Enrollment in health and other benefits is time-limited, so note the deadline you are given and act before it closes.

In the afternoon, connect with your team. Your manager will walk you through your role expectations for the first 30 days, introduce your onboarding buddy, and add you to the recurring team meetings and the channels you need. Ask your manager to point you to the team's working agreements and where documentation lives. Meeting your buddy early matters: this is the person you can ask the small questions that feel too minor to escalate.

Before you log off, complete the administrative closeout. Confirm that your payroll record shows the correct start date and legal name, that your emergency contact is recorded, and that you have acknowledged the code of conduct. Check that your calendar reflects your working hours and time zone so colleagues schedule with you correctly.

A few practical reminders for day one. It is normal for one or two access requests to still be pending at the end of the first day; provisioning across systems is not always instant. Keep a short list of anything still blocked and share it with your manager and buddy so it can be chased on day two. Do not share your credentials with anyone, including IT support, who will never ask for your password. If you are unsure whether a request is legitimate, verify it through an official channel before acting.

By the end of your first day you should be able to sign in to all core systems, know who your manager and buddy are, understand your first-week goals, and have completed payroll and benefits paperwork or scheduled the sessions to do so. The rest of your first week builds on this foundation: deeper role training, meeting adjacent teams, and shadowing live work. If any item on this checklist remains incomplete, flag it rather than moving past it, because early setup gaps tend to compound. Welcome aboard, and treat your first week as a time to ask questions freely.

articles.title: Leave and PTO Policy: Accrual, Requesting Time Off, and Public Holidays
articles.body:
This article explains how paid time off works at Acme, how it accrues, how to request it, and how it interacts with public holidays and other leave types. Exact entitlements vary by employing entity and local law, so always confirm your specific balance in the self-service portal at portal.acme-internal.example, which is the single source of truth for your numbers.

Acme provides annual paid leave (PTO) that accrues over the course of the year. Full-time employees accrue a set number of days per month of service; part-time employees accrue on a pro-rated basis according to their contracted hours. Accrual begins on your start date. Your current balance, your accrual rate, and any carryover from the previous year are visible on your leave dashboard and update at the start of each month.

Carryover rules limit how much unused PTO you can move into the next year. Any balance above the carryover cap that remains unused at year end is forfeited unless local law requires otherwise. To avoid losing time, plan longer breaks earlier in the year and check your projected year-end balance each quarter. Managers are asked to actively approve leave rather than let balances build up, because time off supports sustained performance.

To request time off, submit the request through the portal at least the minimum notice period in advance. As a guideline, single days need short notice, while absences of a week or more should be requested several weeks ahead so your team can plan coverage. The workflow routes to your manager for approval; you will receive a notification when the request is approved or declined. Do not treat a request as approved until you see the confirmation. Approved leave is deducted from your balance on the dates taken, not on the date approved.

A few rules keep the process fair and predictable:

- Peak-period blackout: some teams restrict discretionary leave during known busy windows; your manager will publish these dates in advance.
- Overlapping requests are handled by business need and, where teams must choose, by request order.
- Half-day leave is supported where your local entity allows it; select the half-day option in the request form.
- Leave cannot normally be taken as negative balance; exceptions require manager and People Operations approval.

Public holidays are separate from PTO. Each location has its own published holiday calendar, and these days do not draw down your PTO balance. If a public holiday falls on a day you would not normally work, refer to your local calendar for whether a substitute day applies. When you work across time zones with colleagues in other locations, be aware that their holidays may differ from yours; check the shared calendar before scheduling.

Acme also provides distinct leave categories that should not be recorded as PTO. Sick leave covers personal illness and is tracked separately; follow the notification steps in the sick-leave article and provide documentation if your absence exceeds the threshold that requires it. Parental, bereavement, and other statutory or company leave types have their own entitlements and request paths. Using the correct category matters, because it protects your PTO balance and ensures you receive the right pay treatment.

When you leave the company, any accrued but unused PTO is settled according to your local policy and applicable law, typically as part of your final pay. If you transfer between entities, your balance treatment depends on the transfer terms, so raise this with People Operations before the move.

If you are ever unsure which leave type applies, ask before submitting rather than guessing, because corrections after the fact create payroll rework. For anything not covered here, contact People Operations through the HR help desk. Taking your leave is encouraged, not merely permitted: rested people do better work, and Acme plans capacity on the assumption that people use the time they earn.

articles.title: How to Submit and Get Reimbursed for Business Expenses
articles.body:
This guide explains how to claim reimbursement for money you spend on Acme's behalf. It covers what is claimable, how to submit a claim, what documentation you need, and how long payment takes. The goal is simple: legitimate business costs should be paid back to you quickly and without friction, provided claims are accurate and properly evidenced.

An expense is reimbursable when it is a reasonable, necessary cost incurred wholly for company business and is not otherwise provided by the company. Common examples include work-related travel, accommodation on business trips, approved software or tools bought when the standard catalog process was unavailable, and client-related costs where a policy allows them. Personal costs, commuting to your normal workplace, and anything already covered by a company card or a supplier invoice are not reimbursable through this process.

Before you spend, check whether pre-approval is required. Larger costs, any travel, and anything unusual should be approved by your manager in advance. Pre-approval protects you: if a cost is questioned later, an approval on record resolves it immediately. For small routine amounts under the threshold published in the expense tool, you may claim without prior sign-off, but you still need evidence.

Submit claims in the expense portal at expenses.acme-internal.example. Each line item needs the date, the amount and currency, the category, a short business-purpose note, and an attached receipt. Follow these evidence rules:

- Attach an itemized receipt, not just a card slip, so the category and tax can be verified.
- For foreign-currency spend, submit the original amount; the tool applies the conversion, or you attach the statement showing the charged amount.
- If a receipt is genuinely lost, complete the missing-receipt declaration; repeated use of this option will be queried.
- Group a trip's costs into one claim where possible so approval and payment happen together.

Write the business purpose as if a reviewer who was not there needs to understand it, because that is exactly the case. "Taxi" is weak; "Taxi from airport to client site for onboarding workshop" is clear and approvable. Vague purposes are the most common reason claims are sent back.

After submission, your claim routes to your manager for approval and then to Finance for payment. Managers check that the cost is legitimate and within policy; Finance checks evidence, tax treatment, and coding. If either has a question, the claim returns to you with a comment. Respond promptly, because a returned claim does not progress until you act on it.

Reimbursement is paid to your registered bank account on the standard payment run. As a guideline, a correctly submitted and approved claim is paid within the next scheduled cycle; incomplete claims take longer purely because of the back-and-forth. Submit claims promptly rather than saving them up, and note that there is a submission deadline after which old expenses may not be accepted without an exception.

A few policy points to keep you compliant. Do not split a single purchase across multiple claims to stay under an approval threshold. Do not claim for other people's personal costs; where a shared meal is genuinely a business cost, name the attendees and the purpose. Alcohol, upgrades, and premium options are treated conservatively and may be partially declined. If your local entity has specific limits or tax rules, those override the general guidance here, and the expense tool will usually enforce them for you.

If you are unsure whether something is claimable, ask Finance before you spend, not after. It is far easier to confirm eligibility up front than to argue a declined claim later. For questions about a specific claim, use the comment thread on that claim so the history stays in one place; for general policy questions, contact the Finance help desk. Handled this way, expenses are a routine administrative task rather than a source of stress.

articles.title: The Performance Review Cycle: Timeline, Ratings, and How to Prepare
articles.body:
Acme runs a structured performance review cycle so that feedback, development, and recognition happen on a predictable rhythm rather than ad hoc. This article explains the cycle timeline, the inputs that feed a review, how outcomes are decided, and how to prepare so the conversation is useful to you.

The cycle runs on a regular cadence with two main touchpoints: a lighter mid-cycle check-in and a fuller end-of-cycle review. The mid-cycle check-in is forward-looking: it confirms that your goals still make sense, surfaces blockers, and course-corrects early. The end-of-cycle review looks back at the period as a whole, sets an overall assessment, and feeds decisions about development and, where applicable, compensation and progression. Exact dates are published each cycle in the People portal at portal.acme-internal.example; watch for the announcement, because deadlines for self-assessment and peer input are firm.

Several inputs come together in a review. You complete a self-assessment describing what you delivered against your goals and how you worked. Your manager writes their assessment. Peer feedback is gathered from a small set of colleagues you worked with closely, and where relevant, feedback from people you supported or led. The point of multiple inputs is to reduce single-viewpoint bias and to recognize contributions that one person might not see.

Goals are the backbone of the review, so they should be set well before the cycle closes, not written retroactively. Good goals are specific and tied to outcomes rather than activity, and they include both what you deliver and how you grow. If your goals drifted during the period because priorities changed, note that explicitly in your self-assessment; changing circumstances are a normal part of the story, and a review that ignores them is less accurate.

To prepare well, do a few things ahead of time:

- Keep a running record through the cycle of what you shipped, problems you solved, and feedback you received, so you are not reconstructing months from memory.
- Choose peer reviewers who saw your actual work, and give them enough notice.
- Write your self-assessment with evidence, not adjectives: link to the work and describe the impact.
- Come to the conversation with questions about your development, not only your rating.

Ratings summarize the period against expectations for your role and level. They are meant to be a shared, evidence-based conclusion, and your manager should be able to explain the reasoning behind yours. Calibration is part of the process: managers compare assessments across a group to keep standards consistent, so an individual rating reflects a fair comparison rather than one manager's habits. If your rating surprises you, ask for the specific examples behind it; a rating you cannot connect to concrete work is not useful, and you are entitled to that clarity.

The review conversation itself should be a two-way discussion, not a verdict read aloud. Expect to talk about what went well, what to build on, where you fell short, and what support you need next. Development planning is a required output: you and your manager agree on a small number of focus areas and the concrete steps and support attached to them. Vague development goals with no actions rarely lead anywhere, so push for specifics.

After the cycle closes, outcomes are recorded in the portal, and any decisions that follow (development plans, and where relevant progression or compensation) are communicated through the appropriate channel and timeline. Keep your own copy of the agreed development plan and revisit it during the next mid-cycle check-in, because a plan no one looks at until the following review has done nothing.

A note on fairness and tone: reviews assess work and behaviors, not personality. Feedback should be specific, actionable, and respectful, and it flows in both directions. If you feel a review was conducted unfairly or not in line with this process, raise it with your manager first and, if unresolved, with People Operations. Handled well, the cycle is less an evaluation to survive and more a scheduled chance to be seen accurately and to plan your growth deliberately.

articles.title: Employee Referral Program: How to Refer a Candidate and Earn a Bonus
articles.body:
Acme's employee referral program invites you to recommend people you would want to work with. Referrals consistently produce strong hires because you understand both the work and the person, and the program rewards you when a referral is hired and stays. This article explains who can refer, how to submit a referral, how the bonus works, and the rules that keep the process fair.

Most employees are eligible to make referrals. People directly involved in a given hiring decision, such as the hiring manager or a recruiter working the role, cannot claim a referral bonus for that role, because they are part of the selection process. If you are unsure whether a conflict applies to you, ask the Talent team before submitting. There is no limit on how many people you may refer, and referrals across different teams and locations are welcome.

To refer someone, use the referral portal at careers.acme-internal.example. Submit the candidate's details and the role you think fits, and add a short note on why you think they are a strong match. That note matters more than people expect: a specific recommendation describing how you know the person and what they are good at helps the recruiter far more than a bare name. Always ask the person's permission before submitting them, both out of courtesy and because the recruiter will contact them.

Once submitted, your referral is credited to you and enters the normal hiring process. The candidate is assessed against the same criteria as every other applicant; a referral earns a closer look and a faster first response, but it does not bypass evaluation. You will be able to see status updates for your referral in the portal. Please respect the candidate's confidentiality and do not pressure the hiring team for decisions or push for a specific outcome.

The referral bonus is paid when your referred candidate is hired and completes an initial retention period in the role. Key points about how it works:

- The bonus is tied to a successful hire who stays past the qualifying period, not to the interview alone.
- Amounts can vary by role type and difficulty to fill; the current schedule is published in the referral portal.
- Payment is made through payroll and is subject to normal tax treatment for your location.
- If two employees refer the same person, credit generally goes to the first valid referral on record.

Timing and attribution rules prevent disputes. A referral must be on record before the candidate is already in an active process through another channel; you cannot claim a bonus for someone who had already applied directly or was already being sourced. If a candidate you referred is not hired for the role you suggested but is hired for another within a defined window, your referral may still qualify, so it is worth referring good people even when the immediate fit is imperfect.

There are limits on who counts. Rehires, temporary or contingent staff converting to permanent roles, and senior executive appointments handled through dedicated search are typically excluded; the current exclusions are listed in the program terms. Referring yourself, or arrangements designed to split or game the bonus, are not permitted and will disqualify the referral.

A word on quality over quantity. The program works best when you refer people you would genuinely vouch for, not everyone you have ever met. Thoughtful referrals protect your credibility with the Talent team and make each of your future referrals count for more. Diversity of background strengthens the company, so consider people from outside your immediate circle as well.

If you have questions about eligibility, the current bonus schedule, or the status of a specific referral, contact the Talent team through the careers portal. Full program terms, including qualifying periods and exclusions, live alongside the submission form so you can check the details before you refer. Thank you for helping Acme grow through the people you trust.

articles.title: Remote Work Allowance: Eligibility, What It Covers, and How to Claim
articles.body:
Acme supports remote and hybrid working and provides a remote work allowance to help you set up a safe, productive home workspace. This article explains who is eligible, what the allowance covers, how to claim it, and the responsibilities that come with working away from an office. Specific amounts and rules vary by employing entity and local law, so confirm your figures in the self-service portal at portal.acme-internal.example.

Eligibility follows your working arrangement as agreed with your manager. Employees whose role is designated remote or hybrid qualify for the allowance; fully office-based roles generally do not, because their workspace is provided on site. If your arrangement changes, your eligibility updates from the effective date of that change. New joiners in eligible roles can usually claim the initial setup portion early in their tenure so they are properly equipped from the start.

The allowance typically has two parts. A one-time setup component helps you buy the essentials of a decent workspace, such as a suitable desk and chair or an external monitor and keyboard, where these are not shipped to you as company equipment. A recurring component contributes toward the ongoing costs of working from home. What is covered and how it is paid depends on your location; in some entities the recurring amount is a fixed stipend and in others it reimburses specific documented costs.

What the allowance is intended to cover, and what it is not, matters:

- Covered: reasonable ergonomic furniture and peripherals, and a contribution toward home internet or utilities where the local policy allows it.
- Company-provided instead: your primary laptop and security tooling come through IT asset management, not this allowance.
- Not covered: general home improvements, personal furniture unrelated to work, and premium or luxury items beyond a reasonable standard.
- Not covered: costs already reimbursed elsewhere or provided by the company.

To claim, use the workplace section of the portal or the expense tool, depending on how your entity administers the allowance. For a fixed stipend, enrollment may be automatic once your remote arrangement is recorded; check that it appears on your pay statement and raise a ticket if it does not. For reimbursement-based allowances, submit the cost with an itemized receipt and a short note, following the same evidence standards as ordinary expense claims. Equipment bought with the setup allowance remains subject to your entity's rules on ownership and return; in some cases company-funded equipment must be returned or accounted for when you leave.

With remote work come responsibilities that protect you and the company. Your home workspace should be safe and, as far as reasonable, ergonomic; the allowance exists partly to make that achievable, so use it. Follow information-security policy wherever you work: keep your device locked when unattended, use the approved network protections, avoid working with sensitive information on untrusted public networks, and never let household members use your work device. Be reachable during your agreed working hours and keep your calendar and status accurate so colleagues across time zones can plan around you.

There are practical limits to keep in mind. The allowance is intended for a home working location, not for funding travel or co-working on an open-ended basis; if you want to work regularly from a co-working space or from another country, discuss it with your manager and People Operations first, because tax and legal rules can apply to where you work. Working from a different country for an extended period is not automatically permitted and may need approval well in advance.

If your equipment fails or your setup no longer meets your needs, raise it rather than struggling on; a functional workspace is part of doing the job. For questions about eligibility, amounts, or how your specific entity administers the allowance, contact People Operations or the workplace team through the HR help desk. The full local policy, including current amounts and any tax treatment, is linked from the workplace section of the portal so you can confirm the details that apply to you.

articles.title: Authenticating with API Keys: Creating, Rotating, and Revoking Credentials
articles.body:
Every request to the Acme Platform API must be authenticated with an API key. Keys are issued per workspace and per environment, so a sandbox key can never reach production data and vice versa. This article explains how to create, use, rotate, and revoke keys safely.

API keys are created from the Developer Console under Settings > API Keys. Each key has a visible prefix (for example, ak_demo_ or ak_test_) and a secret portion that is shown only once at creation time. Store the secret immediately in your secrets manager or environment variables. Acme does not retain the plaintext secret and cannot recover it; if it is lost, you must rotate the key.

To authenticate, send the key in the Authorization header as a Bearer token:

  Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY

Do not place keys in query strings, front-end code, mobile bundles, or version control. Query-string credentials are logged by proxies and load balancers, and client-side keys are trivially extractable. Server-to-server calls are the only supported pattern for live keys.

Keys carry scopes that limit what they can do. When creating a key, grant the narrowest set of scopes the integration needs, such as read:orders or write:webhooks. A reporting job should not hold a key with write scopes. Scopes can be tightened at any time; broadening them requires an administrator.

Rotation is a routine hygiene task, not an emergency-only action. We recommend rotating live keys at least every 90 days, and immediately if a key may have been exposed. Because the API supports multiple active keys per environment, rotation is zero-downtime:

- Create a new key with the same scopes.
- Deploy the new key to your services and confirm traffic is flowing on it.
- Revoke the old key once dashboards show no requests using its prefix.

The Console shows a last-used timestamp and a rolling request count per key, which makes it easy to confirm an old key is idle before revoking it. Revocation takes effect within a few seconds across all regions; in-flight requests already authorized are allowed to complete.

If a key is compromised, revoke it first and investigate second. Revocation is instant and reversible only by issuing a new key, so there is no downside to acting quickly. After revoking, review the audit log for requests made by that key prefix to understand the blast radius.

Common authentication errors and their meaning:

- 401 Unauthorized: the key is missing, malformed, or revoked. Check the Authorization header format and that the key has not been rotated out.
- 403 Forbidden: the key is valid but lacks the required scope, or is being used against the wrong environment (a test key calling a live endpoint).
- 404 Not Found on a resource you expect to exist: often a sign the key belongs to a different workspace than the data.

Service accounts deserve special care. For automated systems, create a dedicated key per service rather than sharing one key across many jobs. This keeps the audit trail meaningful and lets you revoke a single misbehaving service without disrupting others. Name keys descriptively in the Console (for example, billing-worker-live) so the owner is obvious months later.

Finally, never embed a live key in documentation, screenshots, support tickets, or chat. If you need to share a reproduction with support, use a sandbox key and redact the prefix. Keys pasted into any shared surface should be treated as compromised and rotated. Following these practices keeps your integration secure while allowing seamless credential rotation with no service interruption.

articles.title: API Rate Limits: Quotas, Headers, and Handling 429 Responses
articles.body:
The Acme Platform API enforces rate limits to protect shared infrastructure and to keep response times predictable for all workspaces. Understanding how limits are counted and how to react to them lets your integration stay well under the ceiling without manual tuning.

Limits are applied per API key using a token-bucket model. Each key has a sustained rate (requests per second) and a burst allowance that lets short spikes through. When the bucket is empty, additional requests receive an HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response until the bucket refills. Default tiers are:

- Sandbox keys: 10 requests/second sustained, burst of 20.
- Standard production keys: 50 requests/second sustained, burst of 100.
- Scaled production keys: negotiated per contract, provisioned on request.

Limits are per key, not per workspace, so splitting heavy workloads across dedicated keys (for example, a separate key for a nightly export job) is a legitimate way to isolate bursty traffic from your interactive traffic. It is not a way to exceed your total contracted throughput; abusive key-splitting to bypass quotas is detected and throttled at the workspace level.

Every response includes rate-limit headers so you never have to guess your remaining budget:

- X-RateLimit-Limit: the ceiling for the current window.
- X-RateLimit-Remaining: requests left before throttling.
- X-RateLimit-Reset: seconds until the bucket refills.

When you receive a 429, the response also includes a Retry-After header giving the number of seconds to wait before retrying. Always honor Retry-After rather than retrying immediately. Immediate retries against a throttled endpoint make the problem worse and can extend the throttling window.

The recommended client strategy is exponential backoff with jitter. On a 429 or a 503, wait for the Retry-After interval (or, if absent, an initial base of one second), then double the wait on each subsequent failure up to a cap of roughly 60 seconds, adding a small random jitter so that many clients do not retry in lockstep. Give up after a bounded number of attempts and surface the failure to your own monitoring rather than retrying forever.

Proactive clients watch X-RateLimit-Remaining and slow themselves down before hitting zero. If Remaining drops below about 10 percent of Limit, introduce a small delay between calls. This smooths traffic and avoids the sawtooth pattern of sprinting into a wall and backing off.

Several design choices reduce how often you touch the limit at all. Prefer bulk and batch endpoints over per-item calls where they exist; a single request that creates 100 records costs one token, not 100. Cache responses that change infrequently rather than re-fetching them on every operation. Use webhooks instead of polling: subscribing to an event is far cheaper than checking a resource on a tight loop. Polling every few seconds is the most common cause of self-inflicted throttling.

Rate limits are separate from concurrency limits. Even under your request-per-second budget, extremely long-running requests held open in parallel can hit a concurrency ceiling that also returns 429. Keep individual requests short, paginate large reads, and stream large exports through the dedicated export endpoints rather than one giant synchronous call.

If your legitimate traffic consistently approaches the ceiling, request a higher tier through your account contact well before a launch rather than during an incident. Provide expected peak requests per second and the time window, and the increase can be provisioned in advance so your launch is not throttled at the worst possible moment.

articles.title: Webhook Delivery and Retries: Endpoints, Signatures, and Idempotency
articles.body:
Webhooks let the Acme Platform push events to your systems the moment they happen, replacing wasteful polling. This article covers how delivery works, how retries are scheduled, and how to build an endpoint that survives duplicates and network failures.

You register one or more endpoint URLs in the Developer Console and subscribe each to a set of event types, such as order.created or payment.settled. When a subscribed event occurs, the platform sends an HTTP POST to your URL with a JSON body describing the event. Your endpoint must be reachable over HTTPS on a public address; the platform does not deliver to plaintext HTTP or to private ranges.

Your endpoint should acknowledge receipt fast. Return a 2xx status within the delivery timeout (10 seconds) to signal success. Do the minimum synchronously: verify the signature, enqueue the event to your own queue, and return 200. Any heavy processing (database writes, third-party calls, sending mail) should happen asynchronously after you have acknowledged. Endpoints that do slow work inline routinely time out and trigger unnecessary retries.

Any non-2xx response, a connection error, or a timeout marks the delivery as failed and schedules a retry. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter over roughly 24 hours. A typical schedule is: immediately, then after ~30 seconds, a few minutes, ~30 minutes, a couple of hours, and so on, with each attempt spaced further apart. After the final attempt the delivery is marked permanently failed and the event is dropped from the retry queue, though it remains visible in the delivery log.

Because retries exist, your endpoint will occasionally receive the same event more than once, for example when your handler succeeds but the acknowledgment is lost in transit. Every event carries a stable, unique event ID in both the payload and a header. Make your handler idempotent by recording processed event IDs and skipping any you have already handled. Idempotency is not optional; treat duplicate delivery as a normal condition, not an edge case.

Verify authenticity on every request. Each delivery includes a signature header computed as an HMAC over the raw request body using your endpoint's signing secret. To verify:

- Read the raw body bytes exactly as received, before any JSON parsing or re-serialization.
- Compute the HMAC-SHA256 with your signing secret.
- Compare it to the signature header using a constant-time comparison.
- Reject the request with 400 if it does not match.

Also check the timestamp included in the signed payload and reject events older than a few minutes to blunt replay attempts. Never trust an unsigned or stale webhook.

When an endpoint fails repeatedly for an extended period, the platform may automatically disable the subscription and notify the workspace owner in the Console. This prevents a dead endpoint from consuming retry capacity indefinitely. Re-enable it from the Console once the endpoint is healthy; you can then replay recent failed events from the delivery log so you do not lose data during the outage.

The delivery log is your primary debugging tool. For each attempt it records the response status, latency, and body returned by your endpoint. If you see repeated 5xx responses, the problem is in your handler; repeated timeouts point to slow inline processing; repeated 401/403 usually means your signature verification is rejecting valid requests, often due to parsing the body before verifying it.

For local development, use a tunneling tool to expose your machine, or point the subscription at a sandbox endpoint. Keep the signing secret out of source control, rotate it if it leaks, and treat every incoming webhook as untrusted until the signature is verified.

articles.title: Paginating Large Result Sets with Cursor-Based Pagination
articles.body:
List endpoints on the Acme Platform API never return an entire collection in one response. They return a bounded page of results plus a pointer to the next page. This article explains the cursor-based pagination model, why it is used, and how to iterate through a full result set correctly.

Every list endpoint accepts a limit parameter controlling page size. The default is 25 and the maximum is 100. Requesting more than the maximum does not error; the API silently clamps the value to 100. Choose a page size that balances round-trips against response size: larger pages mean fewer requests but bigger payloads and longer per-request latency.

The API uses cursor-based (also called keyset) pagination rather than numeric offsets. Each list response contains a data array and a pagination object:

- has_more: a boolean indicating whether further pages exist.
- next_cursor: an opaque string to pass as the cursor parameter on your next request.

To walk a collection, make the first request with just a limit. If has_more is true, make the next request with the same filters plus cursor=<next_cursor>. Repeat until has_more is false. When has_more is false, next_cursor is null and you have reached the end. Do not try to construct or decode cursors yourself; they are opaque tokens whose format may change, and hand-built cursors will be rejected.

Cursor pagination is deliberately chosen over offset/page-number pagination for two reasons. First, it is stable under concurrent writes: if new records are inserted while you paginate, offset-based pages would shift and cause you to skip or double-read rows, whereas a cursor anchors to a specific position in the ordering. Second, it stays fast on large tables because the database seeks directly to the cursor position instead of counting and skipping millions of rows.

A few rules keep pagination correct:
