- Keep your filters identical across every page of a single traversal. Changing a filter or sort mid-traversal invalidates the cursor and produces undefined ordering.
- Do not persist a cursor for long-term use. Cursors are meant to be consumed within a single traversal; a cursor stored for days may expire or point into data that has changed.
- Treat has_more, not an empty data array, as the signal to stop. A page can legitimately contain fewer than limit items and still have more pages, and the last page may be full.

Results are returned in a stable sort order, by default newest first on the creation timestamp with the record ID as a tiebreaker. Endpoints that support alternate sorts document a sort parameter; if you change it, restart the traversal from the first page because the cursor is tied to the active ordering.

For synchronizing large datasets incrementally, prefer a filter on updated_since combined with pagination over re-reading the whole collection each time. Fetch everything changed since your last successful sync timestamp, paginate through those changes, and then advance your stored watermark. This turns a full scan into a small delta on subsequent runs and keeps you well under rate limits.

When building a client, wrap pagination in a helper that yields items lazily and fetches the next page only when the current one is exhausted. This keeps memory flat regardless of collection size and makes the pagination mechanics invisible to the rest of your code. Add a sensible upper bound on total pages fetched in a single call so a runaway loop cannot hammer the API. If you ever receive an error mid-traversal, retry the same cursor with backoff rather than restarting from the beginning, so you do not reprocess pages you already handled.

articles.title: Understanding API Error Codes: Status Classes and the Error Envelope
articles.body:
When a request to the Acme Platform API does not succeed, the response carries a structured error you can act on programmatically. This article describes the HTTP status classes we use, the shape of the error envelope, and how to decide whether an error is worth retrying.

Every error response uses a consistent JSON envelope so your client can parse failures uniformly:

- type: a stable, machine-readable string such as validation_error or rate_limit_exceeded. Branch your logic on this, never on the human-readable message.
- message: a human-readable explanation intended for logs and developers, not end users.
- request_id: a unique identifier for the request. Always log it; support cannot investigate an issue without it.
- details: an optional array, present on validation errors, listing the specific fields and what was wrong with each.

HTTP status codes fall into predictable classes. A 2xx means success. A 4xx means the request was rejected because of something on the caller's side, and retrying the identical request will fail the same way until you change it. A 5xx means the platform failed to process a request that may well have been valid, and retrying with backoff is appropriate.

The client errors you will encounter most often:

- 400 Bad Request: the request is malformed or fails validation. Inspect details to see which fields are invalid. Fix the payload; do not retry unchanged.
- 401 Unauthorized: the API key is missing, malformed, or revoked. Check the Authorization header.
- 403 Forbidden: the key is valid but lacks the required scope or is aimed at the wrong environment.
- 404 Not Found: the resource does not exist, or your key belongs to a different workspace than the resource.
- 409 Conflict: the request collides with current state, for example creating a resource with an idempotency key already used for a different payload.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity: the syntax is valid but the request is semantically impossible, such as referencing a related record that does not exist.
- 429 Too Many Requests: you have hit a rate limit. Honor Retry-After and back off.

Server errors are less common and should be treated as transient:

- 500 Internal Server Error: an unexpected failure on our side. Retry with exponential backoff and, if it persists, contact support with the request_id.
- 502 / 503 / 504: a transient infrastructure or timeout condition. Retry with backoff. A 503 may include Retry-After.

Retry discipline matters. Retry 5xx and 429 responses with exponential backoff and jitter. Do not retry 4xx errors other than 429; they are deterministic and will keep failing until the request itself changes. Retrying validation errors in a loop wastes quota and pollutes your logs.

Mutating requests deserve extra care around retries. If a request times out, you cannot always tell whether the operation actually completed. To make retries safe, send an idempotency key on create and other non-idempotent operations. The platform records the key with the result of the first successful call; a retry with the same key returns the original result instead of performing the action twice. Generate a fresh key per logical operation, not per HTTP attempt, so retries of the same operation share a key.

When you report a problem, include the request_id, the type, the timestamp, and the environment (sandbox or production). That is enough to locate the exact request in our logs. Avoid pasting full request bodies that may contain secrets; the request_id alone is sufficient for us to trace what happened. Building your client to log these fields on every failure turns an opaque outage into a five-minute lookup.

articles.title: Sandbox vs Production: Environment Isolation, Test Data, and Go-Live
articles.body:
The Acme Platform provides two fully separate environments: sandbox for building and testing, and production for real traffic. Keeping them distinct protects live data from experiments and lets you develop with confidence. This article explains how the environments differ and how to promote an integration from one to the other.

The two environments are isolated at every layer. They have different base URLs, different API keys, separate databases, and separate webhook configurations. Data never crosses between them: a record you create in sandbox does not appear in production, and vice versa. Keys are also environment-bound. A test key (prefix ak_test_) works only against the sandbox host, and a live key (prefix ak_demo_) works only against the production host. Using a key against the wrong environment returns 403, which is a deliberate guardrail rather than a bug.

Configure your application to select environment from a single setting that drives both the base URL and the key, so nothing can point a live key at sandbox or send test data to production. A common mistake is hardcoding one and configuring the other; keep them together.

Sandbox is designed to behave like production without real-world consequences:

- It mirrors the same API surface, request and response schemas, and error envelope, so code that works in sandbox works in production.
- It never triggers real side effects: no real charges, no real messages sent to real recipients, no irreversible external actions.
- It provides deterministic test fixtures and magic values that let you trigger specific outcomes on demand, such as a value that forces a declined payment or an input that forces a validation error, so you can exercise failure paths without waiting for them to occur naturally.

Sandbox has relaxed rate limits and is periodically reset. Do not store anything in sandbox you cannot afford to lose, and never treat sandbox data as a system of record. Because it is a shared testing surface, sandbox may run slightly ahead of production on new features flagged for preview; check the changelog to see what is preview-only.

Webhooks are configured per environment. Register a separate endpoint (or a separate path) for sandbox so test events do not reach the handler wired to your production systems. Each environment has its own webhook signing secret; verifying sandbox events with the production secret will fail. During development, point sandbox webhooks at a tunneling tool on your machine, and switch to your real endpoint only when you promote to production.

A disciplined go-live checklist prevents most launch incidents:

- Swap test keys for live keys via configuration, not code changes, and confirm no ak_test_ prefixes remain in your production config.
- Re-verify that live keys hold only the scopes the integration needs.
- Register and verify production webhook endpoints, and confirm the correct signing secret is loaded.
- Confirm your retry, backoff, and idempotency logic is active, since production sees real rate limits and transient errors that sandbox rarely surfaces.
- Run a small, reversible transaction end to end in production before opening the floodgates.

After go-live, keep using sandbox for every change. Develop and test against sandbox, then promote. Never debug against production with real customer data when a sandbox reproduction is possible. If you need to reproduce a production-only issue, capture the request_id and work with support rather than experimenting on live records. Treating sandbox as the default place to build, and production as a carefully guarded destination, keeps real data safe while letting you move quickly.

articles.title: Purchase Order Approval Thresholds and Sign-Off Matrix
articles.body:
Every committed spend at Acme must be backed by an approved purchase order (PO) before goods or services are received. A PO is the control that ties a budget line to a vendor, an amount, and an approver. Confirming an order by email, phone, or verbal agreement without a raised PO is treated as an unauthorized commitment and may become the personal responsibility of the requester.

Approval requirements scale with the value of the PO. The amount used to determine the tier is the total contract value over the full term, not the monthly or per-unit price. A twelve-month subscription is assessed on its annual value, and a multi-year agreement on its aggregate value across all years. Splitting a single requirement into several smaller POs to stay under a threshold is prohibited and will be flagged during audit.

The standard sign-off matrix is:

- Up to 2,000 USD equivalent: line manager approval only.
- 2,001 to 20,000 USD equivalent: line manager plus department head.
- 20,001 to 100,000 USD equivalent: department head plus Finance business partner.
- Above 100,000 USD equivalent: Finance Director plus a member of the executive committee.

All amounts are assessed in USD equivalent using the corporate month-end FX rate, so that a single global threshold applies regardless of the local currency on the invoice. Regional entities may set lower local thresholds but may never raise them above the figures above.

To raise a PO, submit a request in the procurement portal at procure.acme-internal.example with the vendor name, a description of the goods or services, the budget code, the delivery date, and at least one supporting quote. Purchases above 20,000 USD equivalent require a minimum of three competitive quotes, or a documented single-source justification approved by the Finance business partner. Single-source justifications are appropriate where only one vendor can meet a genuine technical or compatibility requirement, not merely because a vendor is already familiar.

Once submitted, the request routes automatically to the approvers indicated by its tier. Approvers receive a portal notification and should action requests within two business days. If an approver is unavailable, a delegate must be configured in the portal in advance; approvals cannot be delegated informally after the fact. The requester can track approval status on the portal dashboard and will be notified when the PO number is issued.

A PO number must exist before any order is placed with a vendor. When the goods or services are received, the requester confirms receipt in the portal, which enables the matching invoice to be paid. Finance operates three-way matching: the invoice, the PO, and the goods-receipt confirmation must agree on quantity and value before payment is released. Discrepancies over a small tolerance are held for the requester to resolve.

Changes to an approved PO, such as an increase in quantity or price, require a change request that is re-approved at the tier corresponding to the new total value. A PO whose value rises from 18,000 to 25,000 USD equivalent, for example, now needs Finance business partner approval even though the original did not.

Common reasons requests are rejected include a missing budget code, insufficient quotes for the value tier, a vendor that has not completed onboarding, and a description too vague for the approver to assess. To avoid delay, confirm the vendor is active in the system and the budget has available funds before submitting. Questions about which tier applies to a particular purchase should go to your Finance business partner rather than being resolved by assumption, as an incorrectly routed PO will be returned and must be raised again.

articles.title: How to Onboard a New Vendor or Supplier
articles.body:
Before Acme can raise a purchase order to a company or pay it, that company must be onboarded as an approved vendor. Onboarding verifies that the vendor is a legitimate business, captures the details needed to pay it correctly, and screens for legal and compliance risk. No payment can be made to a vendor that is not active in the vendor master.

Onboarding is initiated by the employee who wants to work with the vendor, known as the vendor sponsor. The sponsor opens a vendor request in the procurement portal and sends the vendor a secure intake link. The vendor, not the sponsor, completes the intake form; this keeps banking and tax details under the vendor's control and reduces the risk of fraud. Sponsors should never key a vendor's bank details on the vendor's behalf.

The vendor is asked to provide:

- Registered legal name, trading name, and business registration number.
- Registered address and primary operating country.
- Tax identification and any applicable tax residency or withholding documentation.
- Bank account details for payment, provided on official letterhead or a verified banking document.
- A primary billing contact for invoicing matters.

Once the vendor submits the form, Finance performs verification. This includes confirming the business is registered, screening the entity against sanctions and denied-party lists, and independently confirming the bank account through a call-back to a phone number obtained from public records rather than from the intake form itself. This bank verification step is mandatory and is the single most important control against payment redirection fraud. Any request to change vendor bank details later triggers the same call-back verification before the change is applied.

Depending on the category and value of the expected spend, additional due diligence may apply. Vendors that will handle personal data must complete a data-processing assessment. Vendors in higher-risk categories, or those expected to exceed a material annual spend, require a signed master services agreement reviewed by Legal before the first PO. The portal indicates which additional steps are required based on the category the sponsor selects.

Standard onboarding takes about five business days once the vendor has returned a complete intake form; delays are almost always caused by missing or inconsistent documents, so encourage the vendor to submit accurate details the first time. Rushed onboarding is a common source of later payment errors, so plan for this lead time when scheduling work with a new supplier.

When verification is complete, the vendor is set to active status and issued an internal vendor ID. Only then can the sponsor raise a PO against it. The vendor record carries the payment terms, default currency, and category, which flow automatically onto future POs and invoices.

Vendor records are reviewed periodically. A vendor with no activity for an extended period may be set to dormant and must be reactivated, which repeats the key verification checks, before it can be used again. Sponsors are responsible for telling Finance when a vendor relationship ends so the record can be closed.

To keep the vendor master clean, check whether a vendor already exists before starting a new request; duplicate records fragment spend reporting and can cause invoices to be matched against the wrong entity. Search by legal name and registration number first. If you are unsure whether a match is the same legal entity, ask the procurement team rather than creating a second record.

articles.title: Submitting Vendor Invoices and Payment Timelines
articles.body:
This article explains how vendor invoices are submitted, matched, and paid at Acme, and what employees and vendors can do to avoid payment delays. The accounts payable (AP) team processes invoices centrally to keep controls consistent and to prevent duplicate or fraudulent payment.

All vendor invoices must be sent to the central AP inbox at invoices@acme-internal.example, not to individual employees. Invoices sent directly to a sponsor or buyer are not in the payment queue and will not be paid until they reach AP, which is a frequent cause of late payment. If a vendor sends you an invoice, forward it to the AP inbox promptly rather than holding it.

Every invoice must quote a valid Acme purchase order number. This is the mechanism that links the invoice to an approved commitment and to the correct budget. Invoices without a PO number, often called non-PO invoices, cannot be matched automatically and are returned to the vendor with a request to obtain a PO first. The rule is simple: no PO, no pay. Make sure the vendor has your PO number before they issue their invoice.

A compliant invoice includes the vendor's registered legal name, the invoice number and date, the Acme PO number, a line-item description matching the PO, the currency, the amounts before and after tax, tax details, and the vendor's registered bank details as verified during onboarding. Invoices should be submitted as a machine-readable PDF, one invoice per file, so they can be captured accurately.

When an invoice arrives, AP performs three-way matching against the PO and the goods-receipt confirmation. The three documents must agree on quantity and value within a small tolerance. If they match, the invoice is approved for payment automatically. If they do not, the invoice is placed on hold and routed to the requester to resolve, for example by confirming receipt of the goods or adjusting the PO.

Common reasons invoices are held or rejected include:

- No PO number, or a PO number that is closed or fully consumed.
- Invoice value exceeds the remaining balance on the PO.
- Goods or services have not yet been receipted in the portal.
- Bank details on the invoice differ from the verified vendor record.
- Duplicate of an invoice number already in the system.

Standard payment terms are net 30 days from the date a valid, matched invoice is received by AP, unless the contract specifies otherwise. Note that the clock starts when a compliant invoice reaches AP, not when the vendor issued it, so incomplete invoices that must be returned effectively reset the timeline. Approved invoices are paid in scheduled weekly payment runs; an invoice approved shortly after a run will be paid in the following run.

Requesters play an active role in timely payment. Confirming goods receipt promptly, resolving held invoices quickly, and keeping POs open with sufficient balance all prevent avoidable delays. If a vendor chases payment, first check the invoice status on the portal before escalating; most delays trace to a missing receipt confirmation or a non-compliant invoice rather than to AP.

Any change to a vendor's bank details is treated as high risk. AP will never update banking information based on an email or a note on an invoice alone; the change is verified by an independent call-back before any payment is redirected. Employees who receive an urgent request to change payment details or to expedite a payment should treat it as a potential fraud attempt and report it to Finance rather than acting on it.

articles.title: Corporate Card Policy: Eligible Expenses and Reconciliation
articles.body:
The Acme corporate card is a company-liability payment card issued to employees who regularly incur business expenses. It exists to simplify small, routine purchases and travel costs; it is not a substitute for the purchase order process and must never be used to circumvent procurement controls or spending thresholds.

Cards are requested by a line manager through the expenses portal at expenses.acme-internal.example and approved by the department head. Each card carries a monthly spending limit and a per-transaction limit set according to the cardholder's role. Limits can be adjusted temporarily, for example ahead of a large travel period, by manager request. The card is personal to the named holder and must not be shared, lent, or used by anyone else, including a manager or an assistant.

Appropriate uses of the corporate card include travel and accommodation booked outside the central travel tool, meals during business travel within the applicable per-diem, client and team meals within policy, small software subscriptions below the PO threshold, and incidental office supplies. Any commitment that would require a PO under the approval matrix must go through procurement instead, even if the card limit would technically allow it.

The following are not permitted on the corporate card:

- Personal expenses of any kind, even where the cardholder intends to repay them.
- Cash advances, gift cards, or cash-equivalent instruments.
- Purchases that should be raised as a PO, or splitting a purchase to fit the card limit.
- Alcohol where local policy or the specific event prohibits it.
- Recurring subscriptions set up without manager awareness.

Every transaction must be substantiated. Cardholders reconcile their statement in the expenses portal, attaching an itemized receipt to each line and selecting the correct expense category and budget code. An itemized receipt shows what was bought, not merely the total charged; a card slip alone is insufficient for meals and multi-item purchases. Reconciliation is due by the tenth of the month following the statement. Business purpose must be stated for meals and entertainment, including who attended for client meals.

Managers review and approve their team's reconciled expenses. Approval is a real control, not a formality: managers confirm that expenses are legitimate, within policy, and coded correctly. Transactions that appear personal, unusual, or unsupported should be queried before approval rather than passed through.

Unreconciled or unsupported transactions are followed up by Finance. Persistent failure to reconcile on time, or repeated policy breaches, can lead to the card limit being reduced, the card being suspended, and unsupported amounts being recovered from the cardholder. The card remains company property and must be returned or cancelled when the holder changes role or leaves the company.

If a card is lost or you suspect fraudulent transactions, report it immediately: first to the card issuer using the number on the issuer's official website to freeze the card, then to Finance so the account can be monitored. Do not wait for the next statement. Genuine fraudulent charges confirmed by the issuer are not the cardholder's responsibility, but prompt reporting is expected.

Cardholders should keep personal and business spending strictly separate; using the corporate card for a personal purchase, even briefly, creates a reconciliation problem and undermines the control environment. When in doubt about whether an expense is appropriate, ask your manager or Finance before spending rather than after.

articles.title: Booking Business Travel and the Travel Approval Process
articles.body:
This article covers how to book business travel at Acme, the approval required before you travel, and the standards that apply to flights, accommodation, and ground transport. The goal is to get employees where they need to be safely and comfortably while keeping travel spend controlled and visible.

All business travel requires manager approval before anything is booked. Approval is requested through the travel tool at travel.acme-internal.example, where you enter the purpose of the trip, the dates, the destination, and an estimated cost. Approving a trip commits budget, so managers should confirm the business need and that a trip is the right choice before approving; where a video meeting would achieve the same outcome, that is the preferred option, particularly for short internal meetings.

Once a trip is approved, book through the central travel tool wherever possible. The tool holds negotiated rates, applies policy limits automatically, and gives the company duty-of-care visibility of where travelers are, which matters in a disruption or emergency. Booking outside the tool is permitted only where it is genuinely unavailable for a route and must be reconciled on the corporate card with full receipts and a note explaining why the central tool was not used.

Standard travel classes and limits are:

- Flights: economy class for flights under six hours; premium economy is permitted for flights over six hours with manager approval. Business class requires department-head approval and is reserved for exceptional cases.
- Accommodation: standard business hotels within the city cap published in the travel tool; the cap varies by city and season.
- Ground transport: public transport, standard ride-hailing, or standard rental cars. Use airport transfers and rail where they are more economical than flying.

Book as early as the trip is confirmed. Advance booking materially reduces flight and hotel costs, and last-minute travel that could have been foreseen may be questioned. Choose the most economical reasonable option; travelers are not expected to accept unreasonable routings or inconvenient hours purely to save a small amount, but should avoid premium options where a standard one is suitable.

Meals and incidental costs during travel are covered by the applicable per-diem or actual-cost policy for the destination, reconciled on the corporate card with itemized receipts. Alcohol, personal entertainment, in-room extras such as minibar and paid movies, and companion costs are not reimbursable. If you extend a business trip for personal reasons, any additional cost, including the difference in flights and extra hotel nights, is personal and must be paid by you, with only the business portion charged to the company.

All travelers must be reachable during business trips and should keep their itinerary current in the travel tool so the company can support them if plans are disrupted. For higher-risk destinations, additional pre-travel approval and a briefing may be required; the travel tool will flag these routes automatically.

After the trip, reconcile all travel expenses in the expenses portal within the standard deadline, attaching itemized receipts and coding each item to the trip and budget. Unreconciled travel spend is followed up in the same way as other corporate card transactions. If your plans change and a booked trip is cancelled, cancel refundable bookings promptly to recover the cost, and record the reason. Questions about whether a particular cost is covered should go to the travel or expenses team before you commit to it.

articles.title: How to Request and Get a New Budget Approved
articles.body:
A budget is the pre-approved authority to spend against a defined purpose over a defined period. At Acme, spending must sit within an approved budget line before a purchase order or expense can be committed against it. This article explains how to request a new budget or an increase to an existing one, and how those requests are assessed.

Budgets are set primarily during the annual planning cycle, when each department proposes its spending for the coming year against expected activity. Most routine spend should be planned here, because in-year requests compete for a smaller pool of uncommitted funds and receive closer scrutiny. If you can foresee a cost during annual planning, include it there rather than raising it mid-year.

There are two common in-year requests: a new budget line for an unplanned initiative, and an increase to an existing line that is running short. Both are raised in the finance portal at finance.acme-internal.example by the budget owner, usually a manager or department head, using the budget request form. The form asks for the purpose, the amount, the period, the budget category, the funding rationale, and whether the spend is one-off or recurring.

A strong budget request answers three questions clearly:

- What outcome does this spend enable, and what happens if it is not funded?
- How was the amount estimated, and what are the underlying assumptions or quotes?
- Is this a one-off cost or an ongoing commitment, and what is the full-year impact?

Recurring spend deserves particular care because it commits future budgets, not just the current period; a modest monthly subscription becomes a significant annual and multi-year cost. Requests for recurring spend are assessed on their full-year and, where relevant, multi-year impact.

Approval routing depends on the amount and on whether funding already exists. A request that can be funded by reallocating within a department's existing approved envelope may be approved by the department head alone, since the total does not change. A request that increases a department's total budget requires Finance business partner review and, above a material threshold, Finance Director approval. The portal routes the request automatically based on the figures entered. Reallocation within an existing envelope is the fastest path and should be considered first.

Finance assesses requests against available funds, the strength of the rationale, alignment with priorities, and the accuracy of past forecasting by the requesting team. A team that consistently spends close to its forecast builds credibility that helps future requests; persistent over- or under-spending prompts questions. Requests are stronger when supported by quotes or a clear calculation rather than a round-number estimate.

Once approved, the budget line is created or increased in the finance system and becomes available for POs and expenses to be committed against it. The budget owner is responsible for tracking actual spend against the line through the year, using the portal dashboards, and for flagging early if a line is likely to be exceeded. It is far better to raise a forecast increase in advance than to discover an overspend after commitments have already been made.

Spending that exceeds an approved budget line is blocked at the point a PO is raised, which is why keeping budgets current matters operationally and not just for reporting. If you expect to breach a line, request the increase before you commit the spend. Questions about which category a cost belongs to, or whether reallocation is possible, should go to your Finance business partner, who can advise on the fastest compliant route before you submit.

articles.title: Incident Severity Definitions (SEV1-SEV4) and How to Classify a Ticket
articles.body:
This runbook defines the severity levels used across the Acme support and engineering organizations and gives support agents a repeatable method for assigning them. Consistent severity is the backbone of everything downstream: SLA timers, paging, escalation, and status page decisions all key off the severity you set, so classify deliberately rather than by gut feel.

Severity measures customer impact and scope, not how loud the reporter is or how urgent it feels to us internally. Two questions decide it: how many customers or tenants are affected, and how badly is their core workflow blocked. A single frustrated customer with a cosmetic bug is not a SEV1, and a quiet failure that silently corrupts data for everyone is not a SEV3.

The four levels are:

- SEV1 (Critical): Complete outage of a core service, data loss, or a security breach affecting many or all customers. Production is down or unsafe. Requires immediate paging of the on-call engineer and a status page incident.
- SEV2 (Major): Significant degradation or a core feature broken for a meaningful subset of customers, with no reasonable workaround. Business hours paging; status page update if externally visible.
- SEV3 (Minor): A non-core feature is broken, or a core feature is degraded but a workaround exists. Handled during normal support hours, no paging.
- SEV4 (Low): Cosmetic issues, documentation errors, isolated single-user problems, or feature requests. Queued and scheduled normally.

To classify a ticket, start at the top and work down. Ask: is any customer experiencing total loss of the service, data loss, or a security exposure? If yes, it is SEV1 until proven otherwise. If not, ask whether a core workflow is broken with no workaround for more than a handful of accounts. That is SEV2. If a workaround exists or only a peripheral feature is affected, it is SEV3. Everything else is SEV4.

When impact is genuinely ambiguous, round up, not down. It is cheaper to downgrade a SEV2 after ten minutes of investigation than to discover an under-classified SEV3 was actually a platform-wide SEV1. Downgrades are normal and expected; document the reason in the ticket when you change severity so the timeline stays honest.

Severity is not static. Reassess it whenever new information arrives: a bug initially reported by one tenant may turn out to affect a shared component. If the blast radius grows, raise the severity and notify the current incident owner immediately, because a raise may trigger paging and a status page post that were not previously required. Likewise, once a workaround is published and confirmed, a SEV2 may legitimately drop to SEV3.

A few classification traps to avoid. Do not let a large enterprise account automatically inflate severity; account tier drives prioritization within a severity, not the severity itself. Do not use SEV1 as a way to get faster attention on a stubborn SEV3 - it erodes trust in the paging system. And do not leave a ticket unclassified; an unset severity has no SLA timer and will silently age past its target.

Every severity assignment should be visible in the ticket's audit trail with a timestamp and the agent who set it. If you inherit a ticket at shift handoff, confirm the severity still reflects reality before you continue working it. When in doubt, consult the on-call lead rather than guessing. Getting severity right at intake is the single highest-leverage thing a support agent does, because it silently governs response speed, who gets woken up, and what customers see.

articles.title: On-Call Handoff Checklist: Passing the Pager Between Shifts
articles.body:
A clean on-call handoff prevents the most common failure mode in support operations: an incident that quietly falls through the gap between two shifts. This runbook describes how to hand the pager off so the incoming responder starts fully informed and nothing in flight is dropped.

Handoffs happen at every shift boundary and whenever an on-call responder needs to step away for an extended period. The rule is simple: the pager is never unattended, and it is never handed off silently. A handoff is complete only when the incoming responder has explicitly acknowledged it in the on-call channel. Until that acknowledgement, the outgoing responder still owns the pager, even if their shift has technically ended.

Before the handoff, the outgoing responder prepares a short written summary in the shared on-call channel. It does not need to be long, but it must cover the state of anything unresolved. Use this checklist:

- Open incidents: severity, current owner, what is known, and what the next action is.
- Active workarounds or mitigations that are in place but not yet permanent fixes.
- Anything muted, silenced, or temporarily suppressed in alerting, and when it should be un-suppressed.
- Deploys or migrations in progress or scheduled during the incoming shift.
- Tickets escalated to engineering and awaiting a response.
- Anything the incoming responder should watch even if it is currently quiet.

The incoming responder does not passively receive this - they read it back. Confirm access to the paging tool, the runbook library, and the incident tooling before accepting. Verify you can actually receive a test page rather than assuming the configuration carried over. If any handoff item is unclear, ask now, while the outgoing responder is still awake and still on the hook, not three hours into the shift.

For an active SEV1 or SEV2 at the boundary, a written summary is not enough. Do a live verbal or synchronous handoff so the incoming responder inherits full context on the incident's history, the theories already ruled out, and who else is engaged. Mid-incident handoffs are risky; if the incident is close to resolution, the outgoing responder may reasonably choose to see it through rather than transfer it, coordinating with the incoming shift on coverage for anything new.

Do not hand off in a degraded state without flagging it. If you are ending your shift exhausted after a long night incident, say so explicitly, because the incoming responder needs to know the prior shift may have gaps or fatigue-driven decisions worth re-checking. Honesty here is an operational safeguard, not an admission of failure.

After the handoff is acknowledged, the outgoing responder updates the on-call schedule tool so paging routes to the new responder, and confirms the change took effect. A handoff that is verbally agreed but never reflected in the routing configuration means the wrong person still gets paged - a classic and avoidable miss.

Finally, keep the handoff record. The written summary posted in the channel becomes part of the operational history and is invaluable during a postmortem when reconstructing who knew what and when. Treat every handoff as a small, disciplined ritual: prepare, transfer, read back, acknowledge, and update routing. Skipping any one of these steps is how a live incident ends up owned by nobody.

articles.title: Customer Refund Procedure: Eligibility, Approval, and Processing
articles.body:
This runbook explains how support agents evaluate, approve, and process customer refunds. Refunds touch revenue and customer trust simultaneously, so the process balances agent autonomy for routine cases with a clear approval path for anything larger or unusual.

Start by confirming the request is genuinely a refund and not something else in disguise. A customer asking for a refund may actually want a plan downgrade, a credit toward future usage, cancellation of an unwanted renewal, or an apology for a service disruption. Clarify the desired outcome first, because a service credit or a corrected invoice often resolves the situation faster and keeps the customer, whereas a refund frequently accompanies churn.

Refund eligibility falls into a few standard categories:

- Billing error: We charged incorrectly - duplicate charge, wrong tier, or a charge after a confirmed cancellation. These are always eligible and should be corrected promptly.
- Service failure: A significant outage or defect prevented the customer from using what they paid for. Eligible, typically as a pro-rated credit or refund for the affected period.
- Goodwill: The customer is dissatisfied but there was no billing error or major outage. Discretionary, subject to the approval tiers below.
- Out of policy: Requests outside the refund window, or for usage already consumed as agreed, are generally declined - but always with a clear, courteous explanation.

Approval follows monetary tiers so agents can move quickly on small cases. Front-line agents may approve routine refunds up to a defined low threshold, such as a single billing cycle on a standard plan, without further sign-off. Mid-size refunds require a team lead's approval. Large refunds, full annual contract refunds, or anything affecting an enterprise account require manager or finance approval. The exact thresholds live in the internal billing policy; when a request sits near a boundary, escalate rather than assume.

Before processing, verify the account and the specific charge. Confirm you are acting on the correct invoice and the correct payment. Never process a refund based solely on a customer's verbal description of an amount; locate the actual transaction in the billing system. For billing errors, also fix the underlying cause - if a cancellation did not take effect, cancel it properly so the customer is not charged again next cycle, otherwise you will be issuing the same refund in thirty days.

When you process the refund, document everything in the ticket: the category, the amount, the approver if approval was required, and the reason in plain language. This record protects both the customer and the company and is essential if the refund is later questioned. Tell the customer what to expect, including that funds typically take several business days to appear depending on their payment provider, so they do not open a second ticket when the money is not instant.

A few guardrails. Do not promise a refund you are not authorized to approve; say you will confirm and follow up. Do not refund to a different account or payment method than the original charge without additional verification, as this is a common fraud vector. And never disclose or handle full payment card details directly - operate through the billing system's stored references only.

After processing, close the loop: confirm to the customer in writing, note whether they are staying or leaving, and if a service failure drove the refund, ensure the underlying incident is linked so patterns of refund-inducing failures are visible to the product and engineering teams. Refunds are not only a billing action; they are a signal worth tracking.

articles.title: When and How to Escalate a Ticket to Engineering
articles.body:
Escalation to engineering is how support hands a problem to the people who can change the code or the infrastructure. Done well, it delivers a crisp, reproducible problem with everything an engineer needs. Done poorly, it becomes a vague ticket that bounces back and forth for days. This runbook defines when to escalate and how to package the escalation so it moves.

Escalate when the problem cannot be resolved with support tools and knowledge, and specifically when you hit one of these conditions: the issue requires a code change or a bug fix; it points to a platform or infrastructure fault rather than a customer configuration; it is a suspected regression after a recent release; there is possible data loss, corruption, or a security concern; or a known workaround does not exist and the customer is materially blocked. A SEV1 or SEV2 with no available mitigation is an automatic escalation.

Do not escalate simply because a ticket is hard or the customer is upset. First exhaust the support playbook: check the known-issues list, search prior tickets for the same symptom, confirm it is not a configuration or usage error, and attempt to reproduce. Roughly half of would-be escalations dissolve at the reproduction step because the real cause is settings, permissions, or a misunderstanding that support can fix directly.

When you do escalate, quality of the handoff determines speed. A good escalation includes:

- A one-line summary of the problem and its customer impact.
- Severity and the number of accounts affected, with account or tenant identifiers.
- Exact reproduction steps, or an honest note that it is not reliably reproducible.
- What you observed versus what was expected, with timestamps.
- Relevant IDs: request identifiers, trace IDs, error codes, and log excerpts.
- What you already tried and ruled out, so engineering does not repeat your work.

An escalation missing reproduction steps and identifiers is the single biggest cause of slow resolution. If you cannot reproduce, say so plainly and provide the strongest evidence you have - customer-provided screenshots, timestamps to correlate against logs, and the frequency of occurrence. "Intermittent, three reports in two hours, all on the same region" is far more actionable than "customer says it is broken sometimes."

Route the escalation to the correct engineering path. Urgent SEV1 and SEV2 issues go to the on-call engineer through the paging channel, not a queue that is read the next business day. Non-urgent bugs go to the engineering backlog with the severity attached so it is prioritized correctly. Never page for a SEV3 that can wait until morning, and never drop a SEV1 into a slow queue; matching urgency to channel is part of your job.

After escalating, support still owns the customer relationship. Engineering owns the technical fix, but you own communication. Keep the customer informed on a sensible cadence, set realistic expectations, and never go silent. Remain the single point of contact so the customer is not chasing multiple threads.

Finally, close the loop when engineering resolves the issue. Confirm the fix actually addresses the reported symptom, update the customer, and if the root cause is likely to recur for others, add it to the known-issues list with any interim workaround. A resolved escalation that never feeds back into support knowledge guarantees the next agent re-escalates the identical problem from scratch.

articles.title: Maintaining and Using the Known-Issue Workarounds List
articles.body:
The known-issue workarounds list is the fastest tool in support. It lets an agent recognize a familiar problem, give the customer an immediate mitigation, and avoid re-escalating something engineering already knows about. This runbook covers both halves of the discipline: using the list well, and keeping it trustworthy.

Using the list comes first because it is the first thing you should do on any ticket that looks like a defect. Before you investigate from scratch, search known issues by symptom, error code, and affected feature. If you find a match, confirm the customer's situation genuinely fits the entry - same version, same conditions, same error - rather than pattern-matching loosely. A workaround applied to the wrong problem wastes the customer's time and undermines their confidence.

Each known-issue entry should tell you four things: the symptom as a customer would describe it, the confirmed cause or the current best understanding, the workaround steps, and the status of a permanent fix. If the entry has a workaround, walk the customer through it and set expectations clearly - explain that it is a temporary measure while a permanent fix is in progress, so they understand why the problem may recur until the real fix ships.

When you resolve a ticket using a known issue, still record that the customer was affected. Linking tickets to the underlying known issue is what makes impact visible; an entry with forty linked tickets gets prioritized very differently from one that looks like a single isolated report. Silent workarounds hide the true scale of a problem from the people deciding what to fix.

The other half is maintenance, and this is where most known-issue lists rot. An entry is worth adding when a problem is confirmed, likely to recur, and has either a workaround or a clear status. Do not add speculative or one-off issues; a list full of noise is a list nobody trusts. When you add an entry, write the symptom in the customer's language, because the next agent will search by what the customer said, not by the internal root cause.

Keep entries current. The most damaging failure mode is a stale workaround: an entry describing a mitigation for a bug that was fixed two releases ago, still being handed to customers, causing confusion or breaking something that now works correctly. Whenever engineering ships a fix, the known-issue entry must be updated or retired. Ownership matters here:

- The agent who confirms a new recurring issue creates the entry.
- The escalation owner updates status as engineering progresses.
- When a fix ships, the entry is marked resolved with the version, then archived rather than deleted, so historical tickets still resolve to context.

Review the list on a regular cadence rather than only when something breaks. A short periodic sweep to close resolved entries, correct outdated steps, and merge duplicates keeps the list lean. Duplicates are a quiet hazard: two entries for the same underlying bug split the linked-ticket count and make the problem look smaller than it is.

Treat the known-issue list as a shared asset with real operational weight. It shortens resolution time, prevents duplicate escalations, feeds prioritization with honest impact data, and gives customers a consistent answer no matter which agent they reach. That value exists only as long as the list is accurate - so the moment you use an entry that is wrong or outdated, fixing it is not optional cleanup, it is part of closing the ticket.

articles.title: SLA Response and Resolution Targets by Severity
articles.body:
This runbook defines the service level targets support commits to and explains how the clocks work, so agents can prioritize correctly and set honest expectations with customers. SLAs exist to make response predictable; treating them as vague aspirations defeats their purpose.

Two distinct measures matter, and confusing them is a common mistake. First response time is how long until a human meaningfully acknowledges the ticket and begins work - not an automated receipt email. Resolution time, or in many cases a time-to-mitigation, is how long until the customer's problem is actually addressed. Response targets are tight and largely within our control; resolution targets are looser because they depend on the nature of the problem, and for deep engineering issues we commit to communication cadence rather than a hard fix deadline.

Targets scale with severity. As a representative structure that mirrors how most tiers are set:

- SEV1 (Critical): First response in minutes, around the clock. Continuous active work until mitigated. Regular status updates on a short interval until resolved.
- SEV2 (Major): First response within roughly an hour during coverage hours. Active work with updates at least daily.
- SEV3 (Minor): First response within a business day. Resolution as scheduled, with a workaround offered where one exists.
- SEV4 (Low): First response within a couple of business days. Resolved on the normal backlog cadence.

The SLA clock starts when the ticket is created and correctly classified. This is exactly why accurate severity at intake matters so much - an under-classified SEV1 sitting as a SEV3 is silently burning its response target while nobody is paged. Set severity first, because the timer is already running.

Understand what pauses the clock and what does not. When you are waiting on the customer for information you genuinely need, the response clock typically pauses, because we cannot progress without them. But do not abuse this - asking a trivial clarifying question purely to stop the timer is dishonest and shows up in review. The clock does not pause because the problem is hard, because the assigned agent is busy, or because it was escalated to engineering; from the customer's perspective the issue is still open, and our communication commitment continues regardless of who is doing the work.

When a target is at risk of being missed, act before it breaches, not after. Reassign, escalate, or pull in help early. A proactive message telling the customer you need more time and giving a realistic new estimate preserves trust far better than silence followed by a blown target. Most SLA damage comes not from a fix taking longer than hoped, but from the customer hearing nothing while it does.

Business hours and coverage windows apply differently by severity. SEV1 targets run continuously because a critical outage does not respect a schedule. Lower-severity targets are measured against defined support hours, so a SEV3 opened late on a Friday is measured against the next business day, not overnight. Make sure you know which clock a given ticket runs on before you promise a customer a time.

SLAs are commitments, not internal trivia. Meeting them consistently is what lets customers plan around us. Track breaches honestly, review them for patterns rather than blame, and feed recurring causes - a chronically slow queue, a repeat escalation, an under-staffed shift - back into how coverage and staffing are set. An SLA that is measured but never learned from is only paperwork.

articles.title: Data Retention Schedule: How Long We Keep Each Record Type
articles.body:
This article defines how long Acme retains each category of business record and when records must be deleted or archived. Retention is not optional: keeping data longer than needed increases breach exposure and legal risk, while deleting too early can break audit, tax, or contractual obligations. Every team that owns a data store is responsible for applying the schedule below to the systems it controls.

Retention periods are counted from a defined trigger event, not from the moment a record was created. The trigger is usually the end of a relationship or transaction (for example, contract termination or ticket closure). Once the retention period elapses, the record enters a deletion window and must be purged within 30 days unless a legal hold applies.

Standard retention periods by record type:

- Customer account and profile data: 24 months after the account is closed.
- Transaction and billing records: 7 years after the transaction date, to satisfy tax and financial reporting rules.
- Support tickets and chat transcripts: 18 months after ticket closure.
- Marketing consent and preference logs: retained for the life of the subscription plus 3 years as proof of consent.
- Application and access logs: 12 months (see the Audit Logging article for detail).
- Recruitment records for non-hired candidates: 6 months after the decision, unless the candidate consents to a longer talent-pool period.
- Employee records: duration of employment plus 6 years.

Backups follow a separate rule. Because backups are rolling snapshots, we do not surgically delete individual records from them. Instead, backups expire on their own cycle (35 days for operational backups, 12 months for disaster-recovery archives). A record deleted from production will therefore disappear from all backups within, at most, the longest backup cycle. When responding to a deletion request, document this backup lag rather than attempting to edit backup media.

Legal holds override the schedule. If Legal or Compliance places a hold on a matter, all records in scope are frozen: they must not be deleted, altered, or moved, even if their normal retention period expires during the hold. Holds are tracked in the compliance register at register.acme-internal.example, and only the Compliance team can release one. If you receive a deletion request that touches held data, pause and escalate.

Who does what:

- Data owners define which systems store which record types and confirm the schedule is enforced.
- Engineering implements automated purge jobs where feasible; automated deletion is strongly preferred over manual cleanup because it is auditable and consistent.
- Compliance reviews the schedule annually and maintains legal holds.

Automated deletion should emit a log entry recording the record type, the number of records affected, and the run timestamp. Do not log the deleted content itself. These deletion logs are themselves retained for 24 months as evidence that the schedule was applied.

When a new system or data set is introduced, the owning team must map it to an existing retention category before go-live, or propose a new category to Compliance. Storing data with no assigned retention period is treated as a defect. If you are unsure which category applies, default to the shortest plausible period and consult Compliance rather than keeping data indefinitely.

Common mistakes to avoid: exporting production data into spreadsheets or personal drives (these copies escape the schedule and must not be created); assuming anonymized data is out of scope (it is only out of scope if it genuinely cannot be re-identified); and treating archive storage as a place to keep data forever (archives have retention periods too).

Questions about a specific record type, or requests to add a new category, go to the Compliance team through the intake form at requests.acme-internal.example. Do not invent local retention rules for a single team, because inconsistent periods across systems are exactly what auditors flag.

articles.title: How to Handle a Data Subject Access Request (DSAR) End to End
articles.body:
A data subject access request (DSAR) is a request from an individual to see, correct, export, or delete the personal data we hold about them. This article explains how to recognize, log, and fulfill a DSAR within our committed timeline. Handling DSARs correctly is both a legal obligation and a trust signal to customers, so treat every request seriously even when it arrives informally.

Recognize the request first. A DSAR does not have to use the words "data subject access request." Any message where a person asks for a copy of their data, asks what we know about them, or asks us to erase or fix their information is a DSAR. Requests can arrive through support, sales, social channels, or directly by email. Whoever receives one must forward it to the privacy intake queue at privacy.acme-internal.example the same day. Do not attempt to answer it yourself from the front line.

Verify identity before disclosing anything. Releasing personal data to the wrong person is itself a data breach. Verification should be proportionate: for an existing account, confirmation through the account's authenticated session or registered channel is usually sufficient. Never ask the requester to send scanned identity documents unless the risk clearly warrants it, and never store such documents longer than needed to verify.

The standard timeline is 30 calendar days from verified receipt. If a request is complex or we receive many at once, the deadline may be extended once, by up to a further 30 days, but only with Compliance approval and only if we notify the requester of the extension and the reason before the original deadline.

The fulfillment steps are:

- Log the request in the DSAR register with a unique reference and the verified receipt date.
- Classify the request type: access (copy), rectification (correction), erasure (deletion), portability (machine-readable export), or restriction.
- Search all systems in scope using the data map. This includes production databases, the data warehouse, support tools, marketing platforms, and any team spreadsheets known to hold personal data.
- Assemble the response, redacting information about other people that may be mixed into the same records.
- Have Compliance review before release.
- Deliver through a secure channel and record the completion date.

Erasure requests need special care. Deletion must propagate to backups on their normal expiry cycle (documented in the Data Retention Schedule article); explain this lag to the requester rather than claiming instant erasure everywhere. Some data cannot be erased on request, for example transaction records we must keep for tax law. In those cases, restrict the data instead of deleting it and explain the legal basis to the requester.

Third parties matter. If we shared the person's data with processors or vendors, an erasure or rectification request must be passed to them too. The vendor list and their contact routes are maintained alongside the DPA register.

Watch for these pitfalls: disclosing other people's data hidden inside the requester's records; missing data held in shadow spreadsheets outside the official systems; and letting the clock run because the request sat unread in a shared inbox. The 30-day deadline starts at receipt, not at the moment someone finally notices the request.

Every DSAR and its outcome are recorded for 24 months so we can demonstrate we responded properly. If a requester is dissatisfied with our response, escalate to Compliance, who will handle any regulator correspondence. Front-line staff should never negotiate the scope of a request or promise outcomes on their own. When in doubt about whether a message qualifies as a DSAR, forward it to the privacy queue anyway; over-reporting is safe, silently dropping a request is not.

articles.title: Audit Logging Standard: What Events We Log and Why
articles.body:
Audit logs are the record of who did what, where, and when across Acme systems. They exist so that we can investigate incidents, prove compliance, and reconstruct events after the fact. This standard defines which events must be logged, what each log entry must contain, how logs are protected, and how long they are kept. It applies to every service that handles customer data or controls access.

An audit log is different from an application debug log. Debug logs help developers understand behavior and can be verbose and short-lived. Audit logs are a controlled evidence trail: they must be complete, tamper-resistant, and retained on a fixed schedule. Do not mix the two streams. Sensitive security events belong in the audit stream even if they also appear in debug output.

Events that must be logged include:

- Authentication events: successful and failed logins, logouts, password and MFA changes.
- Authorization changes: granting or revoking roles, permissions, or group membership.
- Access to sensitive data: reads and exports of records classified Confidential or Restricted.
- Administrative actions: configuration changes, feature flag toggles, and account provisioning or deprovisioning.
- Data lifecycle events: bulk deletions, retention purges, and legal-hold placement or release.

Each audit entry must contain a consistent minimum set of fields: a timestamp in UTC, the actor identity (a stable user or service identifier), the action performed, the target resource, the source (such as an IP or service name), and the outcome (success or failure). Where an action was performed on behalf of someone else, record both the acting identity and the principal.

Do not log secrets or raw sensitive content. Audit logs prove that an action happened; they should not become a second copy of the data. Never write passwords, tokens, full card or identity numbers, or message bodies into an audit entry. If you must reference a record, log its identifier, not its contents. Logging sensitive payloads turns the audit trail itself into a high-value target and a compliance liability.

Integrity is the point of an audit log, so it must be protected against tampering. Audit streams are written to append-only storage, access to read them is itself restricted and logged, and no one, including administrators, may edit or selectively delete individual entries. If a bug produces bad entries, correct it by appending a documented correction, not by rewriting history.

Audit logs are retained for 12 months in readily searchable storage, after which they may move to cold archive for a further period defined by the record type. Logs under a legal hold are frozen until the hold is released. Retention of the logs themselves is enforced by automated expiry, and those expiry runs are, in turn, logged.

Monitoring makes logs useful in real time. Certain events should trigger alerts rather than sit unread: repeated failed logins for one account, privilege escalations outside change windows, and bulk exports of Restricted data. Alert thresholds are owned by the security team and reviewed quarterly.

When you build or change a service, treat audit logging as part of the feature, not an afterthought. Before a service handling sensitive data goes live, confirm that the required event types are emitted, that entries contain the mandatory fields, and that no sensitive payloads leak into the stream. During incident response, the first question is almost always "what do the audit logs show," and a gap in coverage discovered mid-incident is far more costly than one caught in review. Questions on coverage or field format go to the security team through the standard request channel.

articles.title: Access Provisioning and Deprovisioning: Joiners, Movers, and Leavers
articles.body:
This article defines how access to Acme systems is granted when someone joins or changes role, and how it is removed when they leave. Stale and excessive access is one of the most common findings in security audits, so we manage access through a defined lifecycle rather than ad hoc requests. The guiding principle is least privilege: people get exactly the access their role requires, no more, and only for as long as they need it.

Access is granted through roles, not through one-off permissions. Each job function maps to a role bundle that lists the systems and permission levels appropriate for that function. Managers request access by assigning a role, not by naming individual permissions. This keeps grants consistent, reviewable, and easy to revoke. Requests for anything beyond the standard role require documented justification and approval from the system owner.

The joiner process starts before day one. The hiring manager submits the new starter's role through the access request system at access.acme-internal.example. Provisioning is completed so that baseline access (identity, email, and core tools) is ready on the start date, while access to sensitive systems is activated only once required onboarding and training are complete. Never share a colleague's credentials to give a new joiner a head start; every person has their own identity so that audit logs stay meaningful.

The mover process is where risk quietly accumulates. When someone changes role, new access is added but old access is often forgotten, and over time people collect permissions far beyond their current job. To prevent this, a role change triggers a full re-evaluation: the new role bundle is applied and access tied to the previous role is removed. A move is treated as a leaver-from-the-old-role plus a joiner-to-the-new-role, not simply an addition.

The leaver process must be prompt and complete:

- On the departure date, all access is revoked and active sessions are terminated.
- Accounts are disabled rather than deleted immediately, so that audit history and owned data remain traceable.
- Any shared or service credentials the person knew are rotated.
- Company data on personal or mobile devices is removed.
- Ownership of records, tickets, and documents is reassigned to a named successor.

Timing matters most for privileged and remote access. High-risk access (administrative rights, production systems, VPN) must be revoked immediately on departure, ideally within the same hour, especially for involuntary departures. Baseline account disabling should complete the same business day. HR and the system owners coordinate so the leaver signal reaches every system, including third-party tools that are not centrally managed.

Because no automated process is perfect, we run periodic access reviews. Each quarter, system owners receive the current list of who has access to their systems and must confirm each grant is still justified or revoke it. Access to Restricted data is reviewed more frequently. These reviews catch the residue that joiner, mover, and leaver events miss: orphaned accounts, lingering elevated rights, and vendor accounts that outlived their contract.

Service and machine accounts follow the same discipline as human accounts. Each must have a named human owner, a defined purpose, rotated credentials, and a review cadence. Unowned service accounts are a frequent breach vector and are disabled when no owner can be identified.

Every provisioning and deprovisioning action is logged (see the Audit Logging Standard). If you notice access you no longer need, request its removal rather than keeping it for convenience. Holding unused access is not a benefit; it is a liability you carry on behalf of the whole company. Questions about roles or reviews go to the system owner or the security team.

articles.title: Data Breach Response: Notification Steps and Timelines
articles.body:
This article describes what to do when personal or confidential data may have been exposed, lost, or accessed without authorization. Speed and honesty matter more than blame. A breach handled quickly and transparently protects both affected people and the company; a breach hidden or mishandled turns a technical problem into a legal and reputational one. Everyone is responsible for raising the alarm, and no one is penalized for reporting a suspected breach in good faith.

Recognize what counts as a breach. It is not only a hacker stealing a database. A breach includes a lost or stolen laptop or phone with company data, an email with personal data sent to the wrong recipient, a misconfigured storage bucket left publicly readable, credentials posted in a shared channel, or a vendor notifying us that their systems were compromised. Loss of availability (for example, ransomware that makes data inaccessible) also qualifies. When in doubt, report it.

Report immediately. The moment you suspect a breach, contact the security incident channel at security.acme-internal.example. Do not wait until you are certain, do not investigate alone, and do not try to quietly fix it first. Early reporting preserves options; a delayed report often removes them. Provide what you know: what happened, what data may be involved, and when you noticed.

Contain before you clean up. The immediate goal is to stop the exposure from spreading, while preserving evidence for investigation:

- Isolate affected systems or accounts (disable, disconnect, or lock rather than wiping).
- Revoke and rotate any exposed credentials or tokens.
- Preserve logs and do not delete anything that might explain what happened.
- Record a timeline of events as you go, including timestamps of each action.

The incident lead then assesses scope and severity: what data was involved, how many people are affected, whether the data was encrypted or otherwise protected, and what harm could result. This assessment drives the notification decisions and must be documented.

Notification timelines are strict. Many data protection regimes require notifying the relevant regulator without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach that poses a risk to individuals. Because that clock starts at awareness, the internal report must reach Compliance immediately, not after the investigation concludes. Compliance, not engineering, decides whether and how to notify regulators and affected individuals. Where a breach is likely to result in high risk to individuals, those individuals must also be informed, in clear language, about what happened and what they can do.

A breach involving a vendor is still our responsibility toward our customers. If a processor tells us they were compromised, we treat it as our incident: the same clock and the same obligations apply, and our contracts require vendors to notify us promptly precisely so we can meet these deadlines.

External communication is centralized. Do not discuss a breach publicly, with customers, or on social channels. All external statements come through the designated spokesperson coordinated by Compliance and Communications. Inconsistent or premature statements can worsen legal exposure and confuse affected people.

After containment and notification, we run a post-incident review. The aim is to understand the root cause and fix it, not to assign blame. Findings feed into concrete improvements: closing the misconfiguration, tightening a process, or adding a missing control. The incident record, timeline, assessment, and remediation are retained as evidence that we responded appropriately.

The single most important behavior in this whole process is early reporting. A five-minute message to the security channel when something feels wrong is worth far more than a perfect diagnosis delivered a day too late.

articles.title: PII Minimization: Collect Less, Keep Less, Expose Less
articles.body:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is any data that can identify a person, directly or in combination with other data: names, contact details, account identifiers, device identifiers, location, and more. This article explains our approach to data minimization, the principle that the safest data is the data we never collected. Every field of PII we hold is something we must protect, justify, retain, and eventually delete, so the goal is to hold as little as possible for as short as possible.

Minimization is a design decision, not a cleanup task. It is far cheaper to not collect a field than to collect it, secure it, audit it, and later purge it. When you design a form, an API, an event, or a log line, start from zero fields and add only what a real, current use case requires. "We might need it later" is not a use case. If a genuine future need appears, the field can be added then.

Apply minimization across the whole data lifecycle:

- Collection: gather only fields with a defined purpose. Avoid free-text fields that invite users to paste sensitive details.
- Storage: do not copy PII into spreadsheets, personal drives, analytics events, or chat messages. Each copy multiplies risk and escapes the retention schedule.
- Processing: work with the least identifying form that still does the job. Aggregate, pseudonymize, or tokenize where possible.
- Sharing: give downstream systems and vendors only the fields they need, not the whole record.
- Retention: delete PII once its purpose is served, per the Data Retention Schedule.

Prefer non-identifying alternatives. If you need to count users, count with a rotating identifier rather than storing their email in analytics. If you need to link records across systems, use an internal opaque identifier rather than a natural key like a phone number. If you need to test or demonstrate a feature, use synthetic or masked data, never a copy of real customer records. Production PII must never flow into test, staging, or demo environments.

Be especially careful with logs, analytics, and support tooling, because these are where PII leaks quietly. Debug logs that dump full request bodies, analytics events tagged with email addresses, and support screenshots containing other customers' data are all common findings. Before adding a log line or an event, ask whether it contains PII, and if so, whether an identifier or a hashed value would serve just as well.

Sensitive categories deserve extra restraint. Data such as government identifiers, financial details, health information, or precise location carries higher risk and stricter legal treatment. Do not collect these unless there is a clear, approved need, and never store more precision than required. If you only need to know a person's country, do not store their exact address.

Minimization also makes other obligations easier. DSARs are simpler to fulfill when there are fewer places to search. Breach impact is smaller when less data exists to expose. Retention is cheaper to enforce over fewer fields. In this sense, minimization is not a constraint on the product; it is what makes the rest of our compliance program tractable.

When you are unsure whether a field is needed, default to not collecting it and raise the question with the data owner or Compliance. Adding a justified field later is straightforward; explaining to a regulator why you collected data you never used is not. Review your own systems periodically and ask a simple question of each PII field: do we still need this, and if not, can we stop collecting it and delete what we hold?

articles.title: How to Qualify a Lead Using BANT
articles.body:
BANT is the baseline qualification framework every Account Executive at Acme uses before a lead is promoted from Marketing Qualified Lead (MQL) to Sales Qualified Lead (SQL). BANT stands for Budget, Authority, Need, and Timeline. A lead should not enter the active pipeline until at least three of the four dimensions have a documented answer in the CRM opportunity record.

The goal of BANT is not to disqualify aggressively. It is to make sure reps spend their limited hours on deals that can realistically close within the forecast horizon. A lead that fails BANT today is not dead; it is routed back to nurture and re-scored automatically after 60 days.

Work through the four dimensions in the discovery call:

- Budget: Does the prospect have funds allocated, or a credible path to allocation this fiscal year? Capture a range, not a single number. If budget is unknown, ask who owns the budget line.
- Authority: Who signs, and who can veto? Identify the economic buyer and at least one champion. Single-threaded deals are a top reason for slipped forecasts.
- Need: What measurable problem does the prospect want solved, and what happens if they do nothing? Tie the need to a business metric such as cost per ticket or churn rate.
- Timeline: Is there a compelling event — a contract expiry, an audit, a product launch — that anchors a decision date? A deal with no timeline is a deal with no urgency.

Score each dimension as Confirmed, Partial, or Unknown. The opportunity's qualification field is a rollup of these four values. A deal reaches SQL status when Budget, Authority, and Need are at least Partial and Timeline has a named quarter. Deals missing Authority are the most fragile: always push to multi-thread before advancing the stage.

BANT is a starting point, not a straitjacket. For product-led or bottom-up motions where an individual user adopts first and budget follows later, invert the order: confirm Need and a usage signal first, then work backward to Budget and Authority during expansion. Note in the opportunity which motion applies so forecasting rolls the deal into the correct model.

Common mistakes to avoid:

- Accepting a champion's word on budget without a second source. Champions are optimistic by nature.
- Logging Timeline as 'ASAP.' That is not a date. Convert it to a quarter and a driving event.
- Treating a high job title as Authority. Titles vary across regions and company sizes; confirm the actual approval path instead.

After the discovery call, write a two-sentence qualification summary in the opportunity notes: one sentence on the primary need, one on the path to a decision. This summary is what a manager reads during pipeline review, and it is what the retrieval system surfaces when anyone later asks why the deal was prioritized. Keep it factual and current; update it whenever a dimension changes from Unknown to Confirmed.

If a lead clearly fails on three or more dimensions, mark it Nurture with a reason code rather than deleting it. Reason codes feed the marketing re-engagement engine and help the team learn which sources produce unqualified traffic. A clean disqualification today is worth more than a stale open opportunity that distorts the forecast for a quarter.

articles.title: Discount Approval Matrix and Escalation Path
articles.body:
